However, when these datasets are private, as often is the case with data owned by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, recruiting participants for each parameter setting becomes impractical due to the high cost in time and money. Furthermore, conventional methods such as grid search are too time-consuming and expensive when multiple hyperparameters are at play. Therefore, this work introduces an efficient, fully automated approach to optimizing machine learning models when working with small, private datasets. It leverages the capability of modern machine learning models to handle small, noisy training datasets effectively and incorporates a fast, low-cost technique for selecting the best model setting among a limited number of alternatives. This approach is designed to minimize costs while providing a reliable model, making it especially suitable for data-rich but budget-constrained applications like advertising. To validate its effectiveness, this approach is applied to two classification tasks, utilizing Amazon Mechanical Turk workers' datasets that could not be sampled from the general population due to their high similarity. Instead, the data were collected specifically for this study and share the characteristic of having small, private datasets for model training. The results show significant efficiency gains with only minor decreases in model accuracy when compared to recruiting participants for each parameter setting. Ultimately, we conclude that a careful analysis of detector noise is essential to ensuring the validity of our neutrino measurement techniques. The spread of rumors can be comprehended through a dynamic process, influenced by precursor information and local factors. Recent research transforms this process into a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model, which incorporates an empirical formula for default thresholds. However, analyzing the impact of location-specific factors on the peak and decline of rumors requires a different approach. By applying a method known as the Karsten-Larsson approach, we successfully acquire the distribution of the maximum value of a stochastic process within a given time frame. Moreover, by utilizing the Karsten-Larsson approach in conjunction with the empirical default threshold formula, we are able to analyze the impact of precursor features and location on the peak and decline of rumors. A numerical method is also established to compute the relevant quantities. Through an analysis of Baidu map data and election data, we are able to demonstrate the applicability of this method in real-world scenarios. A summary of the main findings includes: (1) precursor features that increase the default threshold will lead to an increase in the peak of the rumor, but a similar effect on the decline requires specific conditions to be met; (2) location-specific factors that increase the default threshold will result in an increase in the peak and decline of the rumor; (3) an increase in the rate at which the default threshold is raised will lead to a decrease in the peak and decline of the rumor. For the distribution of the maximum value of the process to be skewed to the right, it is necessary for the diffusion term to be skewed in the same manner. Furthermore, the tail risk of the distribution of the maximum value of the process is comparable to that of a Pareto distribution with a limited range. Ultimately, this method provides a new way to analyze the dynamics of information diffusion, a process that can be applied to the study of the spread of rumors, the diffusion of technology, and geographic diffusion. In addition, this approach can be used in conjunction with other methods, such as network analysis, to further increase its effectiveness. A precise measurement of the Fornax cluster's distance was made possible by analyzing the luminosity functions of planetary nebulae there. Researchers extracted a large sample of 3,870 objects from the SPHINX and Fornax3D data sets, all of which were confirmed as planetary nebulae using a machine learning algorithm. The resulting luminosity function showed a characteristic shape and was compared to similar data from the Southern Galactic Plane Survey. From there, a model for the number of nebulae expected at various distances was developed and applied to a specific region of the Fornax cluster to estimate its distance. The analysis yielded a mean distance of 1.98 parsecs to the cluster's center, with an associated error of 0.13 parsecs, which was relatively small compared to previous measurements. A interesting feature observed in the planetary nebulae distribution within the cluster was a broad, curved shape, which was attributed to the presence of a bar. The line profile of the [O III] layer also indicated the presence of the bar, as well as a smaller, nearly circular spiral structure. The presence of these structures was also confirmed by comparing the distribution of planetary nebulae with model simulations. The findings provided clear visual evidence of the Fornax cluster's spiral structure and suggested a view angle of around 20 degrees when observing the cluster from Earth. The research also offered a new method for determining the distances to extragalactic nebulae populations by using machine learning to identify candidate objects and then applying the same techniques to calculate their distances. The accuracy of this approach was verified by comparing the distances to objects in the Milky Way galaxy and by analyzing the distribution of objects in the Fornax cluster. The study's results for the Fornax cluster's central distance and the cluster's structure were consistent with previous findings by other researchers, although the current approach provided the most detailed visual evidence yet. Recent studies demonstrate the potential of programming models built into hardware, which optimize workload performance by reconfiguring processing units, to reduce energy consumption and boost efficiency. To explore the idea of running machine learning workloads on such hardware, we developed LifeStream, a programming model and hardware interface that maps artificial neural networks (ANNs) to hardware units called NeuroBlocks. By analyzing real-world dataset implementations of popular machine learning algorithms with LifeStream, we found that it achieves comparable performance to hand-optimized numerical libraries like Halide and TensorFlow, which are designed to maximize hardware utilization. However, LifeStream's hardware abstraction and ANA framework incur significant overhead when optimizing parameter settings, leading to suboptimal performance in some cases. To address this issue, we introduced a novel algorithm to dynamically optimize NeuroBlock configurations during runtime, resulting in a 10-30% increase in performance. With this dynamic optimization technique, LifeStream's performance is now on par with hand-optimized libraries for most workloads, reducing the gap to less than 10% in only a few cases. To further improve efficiency, we also developed a method for allocating multiple processing units as a single NeuroBlock, increasing performance by another 10-30% in some cases. Ultimately, LifeStream with dynamic optimization achieved this improvement without sacrificing hardware utilization factors, which are now comparable to those of state-of-the-art machine learning libraries like TensorFlow and Halide. To facilitate future research, we are open-sourcing LifeStream's hardware and software prototypes, including a prototype board and the runtime engine and framework for ANA, which can be applied to other programming models and workloads. This research develops a comprehensive, multi-scale modeling framework that captures the complex thermomechanical properties of polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization, a phenomenon prevalent in polyethylenes and polyesters. The proposed model integrates elements of physics-based modeling, stochastic processing histories, and finite element analysis to bridge the gap between molecular-level behavior and macroscopic component performance. The finite element method is employed to model material responses at multiple scales, utilizing user material algorithms to incorporate time-dependent molecular reorganization. The model includes a phase-field approach to represent crystalline structures and material transitions. The influence of processing conditions, represented by stochastic variables, is accounted for through the formation of preferred orientation and crystallization patterns. The model Exhibits improved prediction capabilities when compared to traditional single-scale finite element models, as demonstrated by simulations of uniaxial tension and notch tests. The results highlight the significance of multi-scale modeling in accurately forecasting polymer material behavior. The potential of this model to inform the design of components is also shown. The presented approach provides a framework for analyzing the mechanchemical behavior of polymers and can be adapted for application to additional materials experiencing strain-induced transitions. We derived a model to describe the magnetic susceptibility of superconducting materials near their superconducting transition and examined its behavior for several specific Fermi surface topologies. Notably, in superconducting TaS$_2$ and Hf, we observed a notable anisotropy in magnetic susceptibility that aligns with previous studies, and our model suggests this anisotropy is topologically induced. A key feature of our model is the presence of a "necker" in the magnetic susceptibility, characterized by a minimum value that can indicate the onset of superconductivity. This necker is most evident in materials with Fermi surfaces that include point-like and circular features. We developed a method to extract the necker's temperature and susceptibility values at this minimum, and applied it to TaS$_2$ and Hf. Their necker temperatures were found to be around the superconducting transition temperature, while the values at the necker itself reveal a marked variation in magnetic susceptibility that may be crucial for understanding the superconducting state. Lastly, we propose that this necker could serve as a critical indicator for identifying superconductivity in materials with complex Fermi surfaces.

In learning systems that incorporate diverse situations, a single model cannot effectively handle multiple contexts. To address this limitation, a team proposes using a knowledge-gaining approach by combining multiple models through a minimal-loss method. This approach focuses on the feedback process by incorporating a teacher that provides corrective feedback, helping the models learn from their mistakes. The proposed multi-model learning process involves two components: (1) an initial training phase where multiple models are trained to recognize patterns, and (2) a feedback-based refinement phase where the models are refined using the minimal-loss method. This approach is presented in the context of a binary classification task, where the goal is to recognize diverse contexts, such as identifying different languages in text classification. The results show that this approach yields a notable improvement in performance, achieving an accuracy rate more than 20% higher than the baseline model. Furthermore, this method proves to be an efficient way to develop a single, context-agnostic model, surpassing the performance of specialized models in different scenarios. The proposed method also extends to more complex tasks, such as open-vocabulary product classification, where it demonstrates a significant performance boost of over 10% in zero-shot settings. The innovative approach to multi-model learning through feedback refinement has the potential to revolutionize the way we learn from diverse contexts. The detection of neutron star black hole binaries through the creation of electromagnetic radiation after mergers remains a challenge due to the uncertainty about the neutron star's radius. However, studying the neutron star's creation process provides valuable insights into its birth properties. Specifically, if a neutron star is born with a large radius as a result of its progenitor's spin and density, it may generate an electromagnetic counterpart through merger with a black hole or by itself if its density isn't high enough. By analyzing the relationships between the progenitor's parameters and the neutron star's created, we can gain a deeper understanding of how neutron star binaries form and evolve. In this research, we explore the parameters of neutron star binaries that produce electromagnetic counterparts, including a particular system that was recently observed. Additionally, our work contributes to the broader field of studying neutron star binaries and their role in gravitational wave sources. Our findings will be shared at the 10th ESO Workshop on Giant Stars, and a more detailed analysis will be published in a separate paper. This research is a part of my PhD project, supervised by Chris Fryer, under the funding provided by the NASA APG program.

The validity of the grand canonical ensemble is assessed for a system where the compression is controlled by maintaining constant pressure, the validity being determined by the ratio of the system's compressibility to the volume. The grand canonical ensemble is found to be a reliable approximation when this ratio is significantly smaller than one. The effects of finite chemical potential fluctuations are investigated and it is determined that they do not significantly impact the validity of the grand canonical ensemble under constant pressure conditions. The relationship between the grand canonical and canonical ensembles is examined and it is found that the validity of the canonical ensemble can be predicted by assessing the ratio of the system's susceptibility to the volume and checking if it is much smaller than one. The relationship between the bulk and boundary scalar field theories in this context is analyzed, it being found that the boundary field theory can be used to predict the bulk field theory's behavior during the formation of a polyype phase transition. We introduce an image processing approach that utilizes linear differential equations to model the coexistence of rain generation and elimination. This research refines the simple rain model proposed by Crandall and Pshenichnov, which only accounted for rain formation, by considering two linear differential equations that represent the creation and destruction of rain cells. Our analysis focuses on initializing the system of linear differential equations based on the simple rain model, which provides a theoretical framework for analyzing how rain areas shrink over time. We apply this approach to a real-world image featuring rain, which affects the interpretation of optical flow. By modeling rain degradation in images, our approach can isolate and separate rain formation and destruction from the underlying scene, which may lead to improved scene understanding in image collections being shaped by inclement weather. This research is an important step towards using image rain models for physical optics and scene separation. Our code is available for download at https://github.com/zyang026/PLRE. Our approach has been accepted for presentation at the CVPR 2022 conference.

We analyze how human feedback on comparisons can be structured to provide efficient learning for complex preferences. By leveraging comparisons, humans only need to assess half the possible pairs of items to determine their preferences, which significantly enhances the efficiency of the reward learning process. We develop models that can automatically generate relevant comparisons to inform human feedback, integrating both structured data and human feedback through a process of iterative refinement. Our approach reduces the necessity for human input during the comparison generation stage, while also preventing circular comparisons. By initiating the process with random rankings, we're able to learn the underlying preferences through a hybrid method combining both structured and human feedback, thereby circumventing the need for human intervention during reward learning. Our results show substantial improvements in learning accuracy when comparing traditional methods to our novel approaches, especially when human feedback is limited. Additionally, we find that generating comparisons in batches rather than individually leads to better learning performance. We're also exploring more advanced techniques to further enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of these reward learning methods. By facilitating efficient human feedback via comparisons, we're one step closer to developing interactive learning systems that can effectively capture complex human preferences. These interactive methods have the potential to learn optimal solutions from human feedback in challenging optimization problems, going beyond the limitations of static reward learning approaches. As such, we're sharing our code and datasets to spur the development of related research. In particular, we're exploring whether similar batching comparisons could enhance the efficiency of other human feedback learning methods, such as policy optimization with human feedback. Three commonly abused narcotics, heroin, methadone, and prescription opioids (primarily oxycodone and hydromorphone), have a historical connection in Southwestern Ontario, Canada. Historically, heroin was initially sold on the black market in Canada, but it soon lost popularity due to its costly and illicit nature. In the 1970s and 1980s, heroin started gaining popularity again, especially among younger users, who preferred injecting it. During this time, heroin consumption began to overlap with with methadone and prescription opioids consumption. In an effort to curb the rising heroin epidemic, many users were prescribed methadone as a substitute for heroin, oxycodone, or hydromorphone. As a result, methadone and prescription opioids consumption exploded in Canada's Southwestern region. Furthermore, prescription opioids were widely abused due to their ease of access and a large supply of oxycodone and hydromorphone. All three narcotics reached their peak consumption levels around 2015. Although heroin consumption peaked in 2015, methadone and prescription opioids consumption reached their peak in 2014. Interestingly, prescription opioids consumption and heroin consumption exhibit correlated consumption patterns. Our research offers a comprehensive analysis of the shift from prescription opioids to heroin and the factors that contributed to this shift. It also includes a joint analysis of the dynamics governing the consumption of heroin, methadone, and prescription opioids. It is intriguing to observe the rise of heroin consumption occurring almost in tandem with the rise of prescription opioids consumption. Our data demonstrate a strong correlation between prescription opioids and heroin consumption. It is proposed that this correlation results from users switching between the two drugs. Additionally, our research reveals that a significant increase in heroin availability contributed to the rise of heroin consumption. A finding from our research is particularly noteworthy: the majority of users who switched from prescription opioids to heroin consumed both before switching. It is estimated that about 60% of users who shifted from prescription opioids to heroin consumed both before switching. It is also found that about 25% of users who switched from oxycodone to heroin also used hydromorphone. It is observed that users who switched from hydromorphone to heroin consumed both oxycodone and heroin before switching. Research has shown that neural models may learn to recognize the hierarchical connections in the English language's syntactic structure. Previous studies have demonstrated that learning this relation hierarchy through a task like logical reasoning can enhance the performance of neural models. However, these studies have been limited to basic reasoning and have not explored how well these models can learn from the hierarchy to perform more complex tasks. In order to investigate this capability, we developed a method to extract a more comprehensive set of if-then relations from a vast text corpus. This extraction allowed us to analyze how well neural models could learn the proposed hierarchy of relation types when trained on a subset of the data. We discovered that both BERT and RoBERTa exhibit improved performance on reasoning tasks when trained on the hierarchy, especially when presented with more complex arguments containing multiple levels of nesting. Additionally, we found that neural models' performance is enhanced when trained on the hierarchy with a particular set of relation types that follow a consistent pattern, specifically those expressed by the subordinating conjunctions "for" and "because". When tested on the entire set of extracted relations, we found that the proposed hierarchy can predict the correctness of arguments up to 73%. We found that this hierarchy is not solely useful for training neural models, as it can also be applied to analyze the structure of real-world arguments presented in written text, thereby providing a meaningful interpretation of the extracted if-then relations. In this context, our method for extracting hierarchical relations from text has been made publicly available to facilitate future research. In conclusion, the findings from testing neural models on this relation hierarchy are promising and indicate that there is a wealth of knowledge yet to be uncovered in the vast text corpus used for this study. Consequently, this work lays the groundwork for additional research aimed at exploring more complex if-then relations in the English language. This research has been made publicly available to facilitate future exploration. It has been proposed that the ability to recognize these complex relations is an important aspect of what it means to be linguistically intelligent. Consequently, a comprehensive evaluation metric has been created to assess the capability of neural models and any other relation learning models in this regard. Ultimately, this work is aimed at initiating a dialogue on the capacity of neural models to comprehend the intricate structure of the English language and encouraging the development of advanced models capable of excelling in this domain. This paper explores the idea of unclonable encryption, a concept closely tied to copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Given an unlearnable function, even an all-powerful neural network cannot accurately replicate it, which poses an interesting problem - can we create an encryption method where a significantly more capable attacker, in this case an unlearnable function itself, is unable to clone an encrypted message? To tackle this challenge, we propose a new public-key encryption model called UNCLONE and a corresponding code-generation function called COPYPROT. This model comprises an encoder, decoder, and a copy-protection module. During encryption, the encoder transforms the original message into an encoded format using a random neural network, which is then encrypted to an undifferentiable format using the copy-protection module, based on an unlearnable function that cannot be replicated by any neural network. This results in an attacker, including an unlearnable function itself, being unable to clone the encrypted message with high probability, given sufficient computational resources. We provide an analytical proof for the security of our UNCLONE model and evaluate its feasibility through numerical simulations. Notably, our approach to copy-protection for unlearnable functions may have implications for the study of unlearnable functions in general.

Sequential models like LSTMs and HRNs are widely used to analyze sentence structures, yet they've only been partially understood, especially regarding how they leverage local hints to recognize hierarchical organization. Our analysis reveals that these models can learn to combine local cues to recognize local and distant dependencies, and that their hierarchical processing reflects the sentence's syntactic hierarchy. Additionally, we find that sequential models can distinguish between cues that indicate local or distant dependencies, and that their ability to recognize long-distance dependencies relies on the integration of all previous inputs. We also present methods for visualizing the models' performances in recognizing local and distant dependencies, and demonstrate the applicability of our analysis to inform model design, particularly in scenarios where long-distance dependencies are crucial, such as in reading Comprehension. Our technique is model-agnostic, and can be applied to any sequential model, making it a valuable tool for studying how these models process hierarchical information. We support our findings with an example visualization of a Hierarchical Recurrent Network's performance on a sentence with a complex hierarchy. Overall, our analysis provides significant insights into how sequential models recognize hierarchy in sentences, and can contribute to advancing the design of these models.

By applying the concept of semi-Conjugation to analyze potential energies, we demonstrate the lower semicontinuity of fracture energies in both 2D planar and 3D scenarios. Our research demonstrates that the elastic stored energy indeed converges to a linearised elasticity limit when the deformation becomes infinitesimally small. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the geometrically nonlinear linearised elasticity approach and its linearised counterpart in 2D. However, in 3D, linearised elasticity exhibits a more complex behaviour, displaying non-coincidence with its linearised approximation. We also demonstrate that considering geometric nonlinearity is crucial in 2D and 3D scenarios for achieving lower bounds in linearised elasticity with fracture. These findings are a result of adapting previous methods to accommodate nonlinear elasticity, using recent elasticity formulas, and applying recent generalised linearised elasticity formulas. We conclude by discussing potential applications and future research directions. This study provides a fundamental framework, addressing fundamental concerns and advancing the understanding of brittle fracture energies within nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks.

In a multi-pass energy recovery linac (ERL), a beam can interact with residual RF fields from previous passes, limiting its maximum current. The threshold current, the point at which RF breakdown occurs due to this interaction, is a critical factor in determining the optimal filling pattern in an ERL. We examined how different filling patterns affect the beam-RF interaction and threshold current in an four-pass S-Band ERL. Various filling patterns were tested using an electron beam with an energy of 1.3 GeV and different nominal arrival times. The results show that the beam-RF interaction and threshold current can be understood through the average magnetic field and the maximum electric field in the interaction region, respectively. We found that a filling pattern with a large spread in arrival times can increase the threshold current due to RF field sharing between different pulse trains. However, this approach also results in average magnetic field sharing, which can raise the beam loss threshold and increase beam instability in some cases. Ultimately, a filling pattern with a relatively small arrival time spread was found to be optimal in our four-pass ERL case. We also analyzed how the choice of filling pattern is influenced by the design parameters of the ERL. For example, in our case study, a larger spread in arrival times can increase the threshold current by RF field sharing, but this effect is overpowered by the average magnetic field sharing when considering beam loss threshold and instability. Nevertheless, the optimal filling pattern may vary depending on the specific ERL design and various factors, and a detailed study is necessary to determine the most effective approach. Our research provides a foundation for a more comprehensive study on this topic. We also propose possible methods to enhance threshold current, such as optimizing the shape of RF pulses and filling patterns through symmetrical pulse train arrangement. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) exhibit complex behaviors due to their multiple varying timescales, making it difficult to convey their temporal evolution through a single value, such as a mean intensity. Our research focuses on analyzing long-term variability in AGNs using a newly implemented image processing technique, based on real data from the Kepler telescope. Over four decades, the study reveals an intriguing pattern in the variability of AGNs, showcasing a hierarchical structure that echoes the self-similar patterns found in mathematical models of turbulent processes. Two distinct fractal dimensions were calculated for the data, with a higher one representing the inner regions of the light curves that exhibit greater self-similarity, and a lower one applying to the overall variability. An analysis of the variables' ratios suggests that the inner regions of AGNs can change more rapidly, while the outer areas respond more slowly to changes. The research also compares results for eight individual sources, discovering distinct variability patterns that align with their specific categories. The methods implemented in this research have the potential to enhance current understanding of turbulent processes in the universe. The findings should contribute to the development of more effective strategies for observing and analyzing the complex variability of AGNs, possibly involving the use of new-generation telescopes that can collect vast amounts of data. The techniques introduced in this research can be applied to other scientific areas where self-similar patterns emerge over different scales of measurement. The approach presents a new way of analyzing variability in scientific data, going beyond traditional methods that often rely on statistical calculations. The results for the three AGNs being individually monitored show that the new approach can capture the complex variability more effectively than previous methods. The study includes visual representations of the light curves for all 16 observed AGNs, in the form of "river plots" that display the variability over time. The data shows that the variability is not uniform across all sources, with some exhibiting significant changes over short periods, and others showing little variation over longer periods. The research introduces a new image processing technique, based on a method called "minimum spanning tree analysis," which can capture the hierarchical structure of the variability by identifying the most recent and the most stable data points. The approach produces a visual representation of the variability in the form of a tree-like diagram, where the distance between the branches represents the magnitude of the variability. The research focuses on analyzing the variability of three specific AGNs: GW Mic, V404 Cyg, and XTE J1118+480, using new data from the Kepler telescope and combining it with previous observations from other telescopes. In multi-agent decision-making settings, agents evaluate alternative options based on individual valuations, which can be complex and hard to determine exactly. Recent research has explored the concept of approximately estimating social welfare's overall value using limited information about the valuations. Specifically, a new approach has been introduced, which leverages structural insights to evaluate the overall value of social welfare by considering partial matching relationships between agents and alternative options. Initially, we analyzed the effectiveness of this approach in scenarios where valuations are represented by bipartite graphs and directed graphs, showing that its approximation quality can vary significantly. In this work, we build on these findings by exploring additional scenarios, evaluating the impact of different valuation types, including fractional and integral valuations, as well as the effect of introducing ties between agents and alternative options. Moreover, we develop a new algorithm for estimating social welfare's overall value in scenarios where valuations are represented by bipartite graphs and directed graphs. The algorithm's performance is benchmarked against alternative methods, which estimate social welfare's overall value using different valuation types, such as fractional and integral valuations, and demonstrates its competitiveness in terms of approximation quality. The algorithm is robust and efficient, able to handle large-scale scenarios effectively. The concepts and methods introduced in this work may also be applicable to other decision-making problems, such as the maximum weight independent set problem, and the machine scheduling problem, and the related source code is available at: https://github.com/yingchun1976/sfw-approx. To identify binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys, we developed an analysis method for the point spread function (PSF). The standard approach to detecting binary asteroids involves creating a distance cut-off between the primary body and its satellite based on the object's brightness and resolution. However, this method fails for many cases. We introduced a new analysis technique, building on the PSF analysis software, CAPE. The software uses the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the image to analyze the point spread function and calculate the semi-major axis of an ellipse that matches the image data. We compared his method with the traditional method, applying it to a list of binary asteroid solutions in the Jupiter Geboids dynamical class. The results showed that the point spread function analysis yielded more conservative and realistic shape constraints than the standard approach. The analysis produced dimensions that were, on average, 10% shorter than the traditional method. The new technique also allowed for better interpretation of unresolved components in the point spread function, providing minimum constraints for the minor axis. With the software, we examined a sample of 10 Geboids, sorting them into two groups based on their orbital eccentricities. The study suggested that the greater the orbital eccentricity, the more elongated the shape of the asteroid. The software can be an invaluable tool in searching for binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys, particularly with the upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The technique will enable the selection of targets that have a clear binary component and the potential to be resolved with the instrument's optimal configuration. The software is publicly available at https://github.com/ksjohansson/cappsf. The code can be adapted for use with other shape analysis software, such as GausseAN. Economists often analyze how individuals are influenced by others within networks, where the behavior of one peer can affect another's outcomes. While conventional approaches assume homogenous interactions, recent methods allow for mixed responses, where the impact of a peer's action may either increase or decrease the decision-maker's probability of taking a certain action. We present an alternative strategy for modeling network effects, which utilizes instrumental variable techniques to address endogeneity in network data. This method is particularly useful for identifying positive network effects and estimating the size of the peer cohort that influences behavior. We apply this approach to three datasets, one each from labor, stock market, and educational networks, and find evidence of positive network effects in labor and education, and no significant effects in the stock market. Notably, labor network effects are robust to different specifications and estimators. Additionally, we find that work experience and education have a substantial impact on future labor market outcomes when shared among network members. In contrast, the stock market data shows no meaningful responses to peer behavior. Lastly, we find that classroom cohorts exhibit increased educational attainment, and this effect is particularly pronounced among females. These findings illustrate the value of using instrumental variable techniques to analyze network data and highlight the importance of positive network effects in specific settings. However, they also emphasize the need for caution when interpreting results that may be driven by endogeneity. Moreover, this approach can be applied to a broad range of network data, including those featuring heterogeneous groups and multi-level networks. Ultimately, this method offers a versatile tool for conducting rigorous analyses of network effects in complex data structures.

To establish a performance baseline for MIMO detection, we developed a theoretically optimal Bayesian detector and analyzed the detection errors for a specific scenario where the signal and noise follow a multi-variate complex Gaussian distribution. Unfortunately, the optimal detector is computationally infeasible due to the complexity of its implementation. To address this challenge, we evaluated other detection methods including an iterative successful detection algorithm and a Monte Carlo-based detector. These complementary detectors leverage the optimal detector's results but are efficient because they only consider a limited number of the signal's possible values. We studied the performance of these detectors by generating random, independent MIMO signal and noise components and assuming the transmitter has full knowledge of the channel. We compared their performance to that of the infeasible optimal detector. Our research findings can be applied to design detection methods with optimal error performance. Additionally, we investigated the performance of these detectors under different MIMO array configurations, i.e., square, long and thin arrays. Our results show a significant performance improvement, in terms of error performance, when using the Monte Carlo-based detector over the successful detection algorithm, especially for larger MIMO arrays. We also found that increasing the number of transmit or receive antennas significantly reduces the optimal detector's error rate. Interestingly, we observed that the optimal detector's performance is highly sensitive to the MIMO array configuration, i.e., an extremely narrow MIMO array can have a very high error rate compared to a square or wide MIMO array. To mitigate this sensitivity issue, we propose using different MIMO array configurations simultaneously, which we term adaptive MIMO, to achieve optimal performance. We validated the effectiveness of our proposal by conducting multiple Monte Carlo simulations. We also derived an upper limit for the performance improvement achieved by using multiple MIMO configurations. Interestingly, we found that using just two different array configurations can achieve up to 50% reduction in error rate compared to the optimal detector's performance. Moreover, we found that Monte Carlo-based detection can outperform the infeasible optimal detector's performance when using multiple MIMO configurations, which can be achieved using current MIMO equipment. Lastly, we found that adaptive MIMO equipment can provide similar performance to that of MIMO equipment with full channel knowledge but without the need for transmitting channel knowledge, which can be an energy efficient solution. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the value of using complementary detectors for optimal MIMO detection, which can be achieved using current MIMO equipment without the need for sophisticated algorithm implementation or transmission of large data sets. Consequently, these detection methods can be an energy efficient solution

A major shift in extension direction and velocity occurred around the Middle to Late Jurassic, with implications for the margin's evolution. Initially, extension was oriented north-south with significant velocity, resulting in the formation of a significant rift zone and eventual separation from Africa. A significant change in direction and velocity emerged around the Middle to Late Jurassic, with an abrupt change to an east-west direction with reduced velocity. This change led to the formation of a different rift system, characterized by a gradual and ultimately successful rifting process. Analysis of velocity, strain rate, and lag time pre and post-Jurassic changes indicates that the latter met the conditions for successful continental rifting. This change is attributed to a shift in extension direction toward weak zones within D'Orbigny Craton, reducing stress concentrations and velocity across the margin. A subsequent increase in velocity post-Pan African orogeny contributed to the ultimate breakup of Africa from D'Orbigny Craton. The distinct pre- and post-Jurassic extensional regimes played a crucial role in the margin's evolution, ultimately leading to successful continental rupture. The findings of this study offer a revised extension history for West Africa and highlight the significance of integrating geochemical and geological observations with dynamic modeling in understanding the complex history of a margin's evolution. Understanding why other players' actions succeed or fail in collaborative games can lead to better goal achievement. We propose incorporating a theory-of-mind approach into reinforcement learning to address this challenge. This involves training separate learner and planner agents to model other players' behavior and choose optimal collaborative actions. By implementing a cognitive architecture that shares observations and utilizes the theory-of-mind models to guide action selection, we improve collaborative performance. Using this approach, we develop a framework for multi-agent learning that excels in complex tasks requiring cooperative action. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach in multiple game environments, including one scenario where a domain expert is present. Additionally, we show that this approach facilitates transfer learning across distinct player renditions. A comparative analysis against alternative methods is also included. The constant evolution of languages necessitates continuous lexical adaptation, 
wherein new words emerge and existing words evolve in meaning. 
To anticipate these developments, it's essential to create resources 
that can pinpoint recently acquired or evolved words. 
In this work, we introduce WordEvolve, a framework for modeling word meaning 
evolution from inception to maturity. 
We utilize WordEvolve to explore the emergence of new nouns in English, 
establishing that it can successfully identify words with changed meanings 
and distinguish them from words with stable meanings. 
The model excels at classifying words with meanings that have only just begun 
evolving from those with long-term changes. 
Additionally, WordEvolve is capable of ranking words based on how completely 
they have adopted their mature meaning and is most effective at identifying 
newly evolved nouns when aided by semantic similarity. 
Through frequent vector visualization and lexical substitutions, we show 
that WordEvolve learns to differentiate between words with changing and 
stable meanings and evolves alongside the language. 
We make WordEvolve available for download and encourage the use of this 
framework in exploring language development and change. 
All code and data utilized in this research are accessible via this link: 
https://github.com/awashikam/wordevolve. 
We have also integrated WordEvolve into a companion paper examining the 
evolution of relational nouns in English. 
In this related work, we provide results showing WordEvolve can pinpoint 
newly developed relational nouns and distinguish them from established ones. 
Alongside these findings, we present a theoretical model explaining how 
words with relations and changes in meaning can be identified by this 
framework.

Our research focuses on understanding how shallow and deep knotted proteins fold into their unique frameworks. Shallow knots fold in a single pathway, unlike deep knots which may follow multiple paths. We've identified key differences between these two types of molecular structures and their corresponding folding routes. Our studies reveal that folding pathways for shallow knots and deep knots are distinct, with shallow knots benefiting from initial state stabilization and forgoing alternative routes, whereas deep knots rely on intermediate states and multifaceted paths. Our approach incorporates the primary folding routes for these molecular structures into their designs, allowing us to create models that mirror their natural structures more accurately. These models outperform existing constructs in stability tests, showcasing significant enhancements in energy minimization and implicit solvent simulations. Notably, our results indicate that folding these molecular structures in silico can produce models closely resembling their native states within a reasonable computational time frame. Moreover, our approach can be applied to various target proteins by adapting their monomers and kinots accordingly. Ultimately, our studies provide valuable insights into the unique folding mechanisms of knotted proteins, their underlying thermodynamics, and the potential applications of this understanding in future protein design. Our approach has already led to the development of better protein constructs, and it has the potential to contribute to breakthroughs in this field. All our models and data are available online for further analysis and experimentation. Our research is part of an open discussion to refine our approaches and explore new ideas in protein design. Our goal is to establish a collective knowledge base that can facilitate progress in this field and promote the development of innovative computer-aided design methods. To achieve this, we invite experts in computational biology to collaborate with us, share their expertise, and help us address the numerous challenges ahead. By working together, we can create a robust, versatile, and cutting-edge protein design framework that can be used to develop new proteins with game-changing properties, leading to potential breakthroughs in biomedical research. Our goal is to establish a collaborative, open-access platform where scientists can share their expertise, provide feedback, and contribute to the development of computer-aided design methods. This platform will feature our protein design toolkit, including monomer builder, kinot builder, fold simulator, target finder, and stability analyzer modules, along with comprehensive documentation and comprehensive benchmark datasets. To initiate this collaboration, we have launched the GRIP (Designing Globally Robust, Intrinsically Stable Proteins) project on GitHub, along with the source code for our protein design toolkit and a comprehensive documentation set.

By analyzing a two-flavor QCD model, where the mass of one flavor is set extremely high, we investigate how the massive Nambu-Goldstone boson generates its mass. Our calculations reveal that this can be understood by examining the instanton liquid sum technique. Additionally, we find that the instanton-antiinstanton pair plays a crucial role in this process. A semi-analytical formula has been derived to calculate the mass of the massive Nambu-Goldstone boson, which can be applied to any system exhibiting spontaneous symmetry breaking. Our research offers a method for studying systems with highly massive Goldstone bosons, which could be applicable to investigating systems of large mass differences in other theories. Recent work in counterfactual data generation utilizes decision models that can produce alternative outcomes for individual cases. Contrary to these approaches, we propose using an inverse problem-solving strategy with a general-form optimization model. This method allows us to create diverse counterfactual scenarios from limited real data, resulting in enhanced robustness and improved generalization performance when using these scenarios for training. Our approach and algorithm for counterfactual data generation are demonstrated through a practical application involving classification of images from the CIFAR-10 dataset. Here, we show that when using deep neural networks, incorporating counterfactual data boosts accuracy from 80.5% to 84.6%, outperforming prior work. Additionally, our method exhibits a new way to measure counterfactual diversity, define a metric for assessing counterfactual robustness, and provide a technique for eliminating artificial data during testing. This innovative approach to generating diverse scenarios from real data can contribute to developing machine learning models that are both more resilient and better at predicting real outcomes. This project has been implemented using PyTorch and Datalab at University of California, Santa Barbara. The code for this project is available for viewing at https://github.com/DBWorld/counterfactual-data-generation. This project has been presented in part at the 13th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Multimedia Network Analytics in 2021.

We investigate how varying the growth temperature and method affects the microstructure of molybdenum disulfide grown on a graphene substrate. Our findings suggest that changing the growth temperature significantly alters the epitaxial domains' size and distribution. At lower temperatures, we observe smaller domains with a more uniform distribution, consistent with a domain-driven growth mechanism. In contrast, higher temperatures lead to larger domains, susceptible to merging, driven by a disorder-driven growth mechanism. Utilizing photoluminescence mapping, we distinguish between in-plane domain boundaries and edge states, demonstrating that these boundaries can hold electrons and contribute to thermal conductivity. This alternative includes the option to integrate MoS2 crystals with other 2D materials, such as graphene, for the creation of novel heterostructures. Overall, our study advocates for a more systematic investigation of solid-state epitaxy driven by surface free energy and thermal stress. This knowledge can be applied to a broader range of materials and systems, enriching our comprehension of growth mechanisms and associated physical properties in nanoscale materials and devices. The next-generation Internet, also known as Sixth Generation Internet (6G), will likely incorporate AI technologies that make autonomous decisions at their core.
For 6G to succeed, efficient management of network resources, including computing capabilities and wireless infrastructures, is crucial and must be done with a focus on overall performance rather than individual optimization.
This concept is known as slice management, which involves allocating pre-configured network slices to applications or services based on their specific requirements.
However, the rapid deployment and varying demands of 5G/6G applications and services require a more dynamic approach to slice management, necessitating an autonomous and online decision-making method.

We also investigate the impact of different compute and communication resource relationships on performance and consider scenarios where application demands change over time.
Our approach is designed for online decision-making to handle changing scenarios and includes a method for monitoring and adjusting slices accordingly.

This research investigates how the presence of an underlying diffusion affects the optimal payoff in the context of backward stochastic differential equations, with a focus on a specific model involving a credit risk index. Our study involves a multi-asset BSGS equation, derived from a backward SDE approach, and aims to determine the maximum possible payoff subject to a constraint, given the underlying diffusion process. Key findings include an exploration of the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the BSGS equation, as well as an examination of the optimal control strategy. Our results also address convergence and approximation properties of an numerical implementation based on a suitable decoupling technique and a pathwise representation. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the importance of considering the underlying diffusion process in credit risk management, particularly in scenarios with default events. These events introduce memory effects into the process, rendering typical scaling limits inapplicable, and thus necessitating an alternative approach to superhedging. Our results provide a framework for superhedging strategies, both theoretical and numerical, and offer a foundation for further exploration in contexts with multiple default events and more complex processes. Lastly, our research is accompanied by a non-trivial numerical example, illustrating the convergence of our approach in a realistic scenario. This research is an extension of the author's Ph.D. thesis, conducted under the supervision of Jean-Paul Laurent, at the Université Paris Dauphine.

Our findings also enable us to anticipate rates for direct lepton production at the LHC in various channels, such as $\mu \mu \mu \mu$ and $\mu e \mu e$. To facilitate further research, we have made our likelihood analysis and theoretical predictions publicly available.

Mathematical models of disease propagation play a crucial role in evaluating pandemic management strategies and predicting epidemiological outcomes. However, models must also adhere to biological plausibility, as uncontrolled growth in some models can't be reconciled with the limits of infectious spread. Unfortunately, conventional least-squares estimation often produces unbiologically feasible solutions due to the ill-posedness of fitting complex model data. This typically results in the adoption of conservative, restrictive models, which lack the flexibility to capture the dynamics of real-world disease spread. To address these limitations, we developed a novel, feasible-environment estimation framework, utilizing a constraint-based approach to limit unbiological solutions. This approach leverages trust region methods in combination with gradient-projection techniques to converge on feasible solutions within a reasonable time frame. By applying this innovative method to a variety of case studies, including COVID-19 data across different jurisdictions, we demonstrated its effectiveness in obtaining biologically plausible solutions. This, in turn, enabled a more accurate interpretation of model-derived insights, providing valuable guidance for public health policy decisions. Our method may be applied to any nonlinear optimization problem with constraints, making it a valuable tool for a broad range of applications. An examination is performed of how an external linear potential affects the statistical behavior of linear Majorana fermions near their zero-energy state. A linear coupling to an electromagnetic field is modeled using a Lagrangian modification. Further, the influence of this potential on the fermions' entropy is calculated using a thermodynamic analysis. Specifically, entropy expressions are derived for situations where the potential has a constant linear gradient and a linear gradient that is directly proportional to the particle charge. The resulting entropy formulas demonstrate consistency with established theories for zero-voltage entropy levels and also showcase sub-Linear dependence on the potential strength. The implications of these findings are explored within the context of Superconductor-Majorana hybrid structures. Moreover, a linear back-bending phenomenon is identified and analyzed in relation to the Majorana zero-mode. Conditions are laid out for the linear potential effect to be negligible in comparison to other entropy increase mechanisms. Moreover, a criterion is established for distinguishing between zero-mode behavior and edge-mode behavior based on entropy differentiation. The effectiveness of a particular control method for the Majorana zero-mode, i.e., applying a linear potential via a nearby Superconductor, is assessed and advised against until methods that only indirectly affect the zero-mode, such as bias-controlled transparency of a tunnel barrier, are fully explored. The conceptual framework developed here can be further expanded to investigate other interacting Majorana modes or modes interacting with varying potentials. The theoretical framework can also be applied to evaluate entropy in scenarios where a linear potential is present, regardless of whether it arises from an electromagnetic field or another force, provided that the force can be represented as having a linear effect on the Majorana fermions. Current methods that leverage learning algorithms for acronym disambiguation are restricted to specific domains and usually require a comprehensive training dataset. Furthermore, existing approaches assume a comprehensive list of possible abbreviations is available in advance. This research addresses these shortcomings by proposing a novel framework that utilizes natural language processing techniques and system-level data to classify and differentiate acronyms across various domains and subject areas, ultimately yielding a dynamic list of possible abbreviations. The proposed approach consists of two primary components: (1) a class prediction model that leverages a system's organizational hierarchy and domain classifications to group acronyms by category, and (2) a disambiguation model that incorporates contextual language to distinguish between similar-looking abbreviations in different classes. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to processing company financial reports, where it successfully classifies and differentiates various stock abbreviations. The system's versatility is further showcased by its ability to accurately identify and distinguish healthcare-related acronym abbreviations in biomedical articles. Our proposed method involves approximating a complex quantum system by representing its behavior with respect to time on a non-rigid pendulum model. This pendulum model helps us understand atom-molecule phase space transformations and the emergence of instability in quantum systems by analyzing the stochastic motion of a point in their potential energy landscapes. We have determined the parameters required for this pendulum model for systems of atoms interacting through various forces, including harmonic, vortex, and three-body forces. Our findings show that these systems all share a similar pendulum dynamics, and that their stability depends on the snaking pattern of their solutions. We have also found that the shape of their potential energy landscapes remains the same for all systems, and that this pattern repeats itself at different levels of molecular complexity. Furthermore, we have established that molecular branches form when the pendulum swings a specific angle, and that this angle is determined by two-body force parameters. We have further investigated higher molecular branches, and found that they emerge when the pendulum swings an even larger angle, influenced by other two-body force parameters. Additionally, we have found that pendulum oscillations can be used to create "molecular breathers", a type of stable molecule that exists for a limited time. We have also found conditions under the kick excitations of molecular breathers. Finally, we have found that pendulum motion can be used to create molecule-atom pairs living in a metastable state. We have applied our method to a specific system consisting of two atomic condensates held in separate magnetic traps by applying a kick to one of the systems. We have found that pendulum oscillations can lead to molecule-atom conversions, and that this process can create molecule-atom pairs living in a metastable state. We have also found that the shape of these pairs depends on the force that interacts with them, and that they can exist for a time comparable to their spatial extension. We believe that our method will allow other researchers to efficiently identify atom-molecule phase transitions and stability in all types of quantum systems. This issue forces the application to allocate storage space carefully, leading to complex management of storage partitions. The problem of identifying optimal primer pairs for dividing storage space has been proven computationally hard. Recently, researchers have identified several key characteristics that distinguish nodal lines in momentum space from other topological states. Firstly, nodal lines must occupy a continuous curve or point in the momentum space, without being confined to surfaces or points. Secondly, a nodal line in isolation cannot serve as a minimum at the Fermi level, instead it either appears in pairs that repel each other or is surrounded by rings that attract it. Thirdly, the pairing between nodal lines and rings occurs through the use of umklapp interband transitions when the momentum space of a crystal is filled. Lastly, nodal lines can only exist in crystals that lack inversion symmetry. This study focuses on magnetoelectric crystals that rotate the momentum space and thus shift the locations of nodal lines without closing them, making them stable. An example of this type of crystal is CoZnO, a material that has been theoretically shown to have nodal-semimetal properties. The amount of rotation increases with the strength of magnetoelectric coupling in these materials. The amount of rotation can influence the nodal lines by either moving them along a ring or creating pairs of lines. The rotation of the momentum space can be directly observed in time-domain through the use of x-ray free-electron lasers. This study proposes that this technique could be used to investigate the magnetoelectric properties of crystals that rotate the momentum space, specifically by following the path of nodal lines as the crystal is subjected to varying levels of magnetoelectric coupling. This could provide a new way to study the magnetoelectric properties of materials that have not yet been possible with existing techniques. Creating High Dynamic Range (HDR) images involves combining multiple exposures of a scene to capture a wider range of brightness levels. This typically involves selecting the most suitable exposure settings through trial and error, or by using algorithms to determine optimal settings. Recent advancements in deep learning and light field technology have enabled the generation of realistic HDR images from minimal photos. However, these methods are complicated by variables such as the shooter's and observer's viewpoints. In contrast, our research focuses on producing realistic HDR images from varying exposure settings, without concerning ourselves with perspective differences. To achieve this, we developed a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns from data and maps low-density HDR images to high-density ones. This network is trained using pairs of high and low-density HDR images, without needing actual HDR images. Our results show that our method produces more realistic and higher-quality HDR images than existing algorithms. Additionally, our approach allows for the generation of realistic HDR images from videos, demonstrating feasible and efficient performance. The technique we've introduced can be viewed as an innovative solution for non-blind HDR enhancement, offering a straightforward way to enhance low-density HDR images. By taking into account the effects of changing water temperature on the proton resonance frequency in water, it becomes possible to utilize this additional information to enhance the effectiveness of temperature measurements.  This improvement can be achieved through a model that accounts for the changes in proton resonance frequency in response to changing water temperature and is correlated with the measured output signal.  This model can be utilized in a least squares optimization routine along with output signal data to refine the proton resonance frequency shift model parameters.  Once the parameters are determined, the model can be utilized in conjunction with the differential equation that describes the time-dependent changes in the reactor and thus provide more accurate temperature measurements.  This method is tested on a simulated research reactor system with a moderate response time and shown to yield superior results when compared to the traditional method.  The degree of improvement in performance varies based on the specific reactor system in question, but it has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of temperature measurements in reactors that operate at higher speeds.  It should be noted that in reactors that operate slowly, the potential for improvement may be less significant due to the relatively small changes in proton resonance frequency over time, thus necessitating a careful evaluation of the specific reactor system in question before implementing this method.  Ultimately, this method has the potential to enhance the performance of water-filled reactors by improving the accuracy of temperature measurements, but it is contingent upon the rate of change of the reactor system being sufficient to take full advantage of the additional information provided by the proton resonance frequency shift in water. This paper builds upon existing knowledge regarding the limiting spectral distribution of large symmetric matrices with independent entries, specifically those that follow sub-exponential or sub-Gaussian distributions. We contribute new findings by broadening the range of conditions under which the limiting spectral distribution exists with probability or almost sure consistency. Our results are applicable to models where the off-diagonal entries may have varying distribution types, provided that the corresponding variance is bounded by a function of the matrix size. We also establish a central limit theorem for the normalized eigenvalues of these symmetric matrices. Our methods employ a combination of localization techniques, interacting particle systems, and rescaled component eigenvalue distributions. We also derive a unified formula for the limiting spectral distribution, addressing a question raised by Paul Bourgain. We examine how the presence of variations in diffusion rates and correlations among particles deviates from typical Gaussian diffusion models. A mathematical approach is employed to analyze the impact of these factors on spatial dispersion. Our method involves solving a linear integro-differential equation, which yields a general expression for the diffusion operator. We demonstrate that in cases of constant diffusion rates and absence of correlations, this operator reduces to the standard Laplacian. A specific application is considered in relation to the spreading of a population with heterogeneous diffusion within a heterogeneous environment; here, we find that variations in individual diffusion rates accelerate spatial dispersion, while variations in the environment's correlation length can lead to accelerated or slowed-down dispersion, depending on the population's initial conditions and its size. Additionally, we develop a numerical method for solving the associated forward problem and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation of real-world scenarios. Lastly, we explore the conceptual connections between our model and both subdiffusive spreading and the blockage of rivers.

Following a discussion on the energy quantization of the electromagnetic field in a closed space, we analyze how the atomic Balmer series spectrum is affected when surrounded by this quantized field. Our approach utilizes a combination of electromagnetic quantization and diabatic perturbation theory to treat the interaction between the atomic system and the surrounding field. We derive an effective Hamiltonian that accounts for the coupling between the atomic energy levels and the field modes, considering the effects of mode quantization and the long wavelength approximation. With this Hamiltonian, we are able to explain the shift and broadening of atomic transition frequencies as observed in atom-electromagnetic field interactions. Specifically, we show that the energy level pattern resembling Rydberg spectra near the Rydberg limit can be understood by focusing on the two-photon transitions between the atomic energy levels and the field modes. For the Balmer series, we find that the additional energy shifts can be described by a formula related to the harmonic series, with the fundamental frequency corresponding to the energy difference between the ground atomic state and the first excited atomic state. This framework provides a theoretical basis for analyzing how the atomic Balmer series spectrum is modified when surrounded by a quantized electromagnetic field. Through numerical simulation, we demonstrate the emergence of Rydberg-like patterns and the associated field-induced shift in energy levels for both hydrogen and helium atoms. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which the effects of electron spin and the behavior at high energies become significant factors. By identifying the role of both the atomic ground state and the highest energy level within the spectral range in question, we are able to classify the atomic spectrum as being of the Rydberg type. Additionally, we demonstrate that the quantization of energy in the electromagnetic field results in a harmonic series spectrum, as opposed to the Rydberg series observed in atom-free space. Finally, we suggest that our approach can be expanded to study the effects of the atomic Balmer series on surrounding electrons within a solid-state environment. Upcoming work will explore this extension in more detail. Our approach offers a new way of understanding atom-electromagnetic field interactions and may provide a framework for explaining certain features observed in solid-state physics, such as the stabilization of atomic states within crystal lattices. Ultimately, this approach has the potential to be applied to a broader range of systems, such as atom-molecule interactions and atomic spectra in intense laser fields. By examining the interplay between atomic energy levels and the surrounding electromagnetic field, we may uncover a deeper understanding of how atomic spectra are shaped by their environment.

Deep neural network classifiers have revolutionized the field of computer vision, serving as a basis for other advanced computer vision models, including efficient networks and human-interpretation-related tasks. Nonetheless, these models are prone to over-confidence in misclassification scenarios. This phenomenon stems from the training process using supervised learning, as the optimization algorithm prioritizes matching the labels of training data. To address this limitation, we develop an unconventional evaluation framework that assesses the performance of deep neural networks in an uncertain environment. This framework treats prediction uncertainty as a core performance indicator and guides the training process using an uncertainty-loss function. By incorporating this approach, we observed a notable reduction in over-confidence in prediction tasks completed by the ModelNet40 dataset. The improved networks demonstrated increased accuracy in both clean and corrupted data scenarios and outperformed the original network when subjected to uncertainty. Interestingly, the uncertainty loss function also enhanced the performance of networks trained using real-world datasets, such as the PASCAL VOC segmentation dataset. To fairly assess reinforcement learning algorithms, it's essential to modify the curriculum in a managed way, introducing ordered challenges that mirror the problem's progression. Unfortunately, existing methods fail to produce curricula on par with human standards due to their lack of connection to value-based evaluation techniques, leading to inconsistent and condition-specific results. To address this issue, we suggest developing a method to create curricula through careful modification of value functions. First, we represent the learning process as a continuous process, mapping the current state to desired future states. Next, we define a distance metric that measures the difference between two value functions, specifically tailored for smooth embedding via convex optimization. By solving a convex problem, we can then derive a method to generate a new state-action value function, closely related to the original, by minimizing the difference between two models. By applying this approach on a per transition basis, we can create a curriculum through controlled value function modifications. Our algorithm produces results superior to existing methods on complex tasks. For example, it surpasses straight epoch baselines on CartPole, outperforms diverse baseline algorithms on Montezuma's Revenge, and doubles the efficiency of learning on Montezuma's Revenge compared to the popular reward extraktion method. These comparisons usually rely on difference graphs that map disparities between process versions, but existing methods only consider static differences, neglecting temporal factors. In contrast, our approach represents variations in process behavior over time using Dynamic Change Relations (DCR) graphs, which capture both ongoing and completed changes and provide a more comprehensive insight into process evolution. We offer a set of operations for DCR graphs, including union, reduction, and enrichment, addressing concerns like removing temporary changes, ignoring unfulfilled changes, and filling in missing data. We demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of our methods through implementations of three analysis techniques: case analysis, performance analysis, and cycle analysis, resulting in valuable process insights. We present Liger, a distributed storage system designed for real-time petabyte-scale data processing. Developed to manage high traffic and large data volumes generated by network events, Liger's architecture combines fast data capture with historical data retention. At its core, Liger employs an in-memory data grid and a hybrid storage layer to achieve high performance and density. These components work together to minimize data movement and retention costs. Critical subsystems like the Data Reduction System and Time Series Database motivate novel disk storage designs that balance data compression and query efficiency. We highlight key challenges faced during Liger's development and showcase its effectiveness with Network Security Monitoring use cases, achieving data capture speeds of up to 12Gbps, a 10-fold decrease in disk storage requirements, and a 50x improvement in query execution times for real-time analytics. By addressing these successes and setbacks, we can provide valuable lessons for designing large-scale, distributed systems. These lessons have already influenced the evolution of Liger into its next iteration, Leviathan. Leveraging the lessons learned, we outline the architecture for Leviathan's data storage layer and outlines Leviathan's data processing layer architecture before concluding with future development directions. This work focuses on the moduli space $\bar{M}_1$ of algebraic curves of genus one, addressing a long-standing question about its geometric interpretation. Initially developed through the compactification of Hurwitz spaces, it reveals that $\bar{M}_1$ equates to a combination of geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications, where the geometric one is represented by Deligne-Mumford's compactification and the Hodge-theoretic one is represented by orthogonal periods, contrasting with the geometric compactification. Leveraging this new understanding, we derive explicit descriptions of the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications within $\bar{M}_1$, identifying them as combination components, particularly focusing on horizontal components. Additionally, we establish connections to; Calabi-Yau's three-dimensional varieties, algebraic surfaces, and the Mumford representation of $\bar{M}_g$, as well as curves with abelian torsion algebraic line bundles. Lastly, we outline the scope and limitations of this study within the broader context of moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. 

This research is part of a series of works that aim to analyze and understand the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications within the moduli spaces of algebraic varieties, specifically focusing on curves of genus one. Recent research applies a novel condition to identify correspondences between population dynamics and underlying mechanisms, utilizing a synthetic ecosystem as a model. This study utilizes a swarm intelligence approach, incorporating multiple interaction scales, to model the behavior of a population within a virtual world. A control system is then established to adjust environmental settings based on analytical data, allowing for the prediction of impending population collapse through identification of a critical condition linked to spatial correlation and variability. When this condition is met, a sudden transition from stable to unstable behavior is observed, and the model demonstrates the ability to forecast a decline in population stability before it occurs. Furthermore, this framework can be adapted to analyze other complex systems characterized by multi-scale interactions and coherent behavior. By applying this approach to data from a real-world forest ecosystem, the study demonstrates its practical applicability. This research reveals that advanced statistical analysis and predictive modeling can be an effective combination for enhancing the understanding of ecological transitions and facilitating the development of more predictive theories of complex adaptive systems. Using observations from the Krylovskaya Telescope and the BOK Telescope, 
we used a sample of 6567 galaxies at z=0 to investigate how NUV-r color 
varies with galaxy mass. Our analysis reveals a distinct trend within our data, 
with NUV-r color becoming a fixed 0.15 units regardless of mass above 4x10^10 solar masses. 

This trend is consistent across various galaxy types and environments, as well as in our mock catalog simulations. It suggests that more massive galaxies are capped in their NUV-r color development.

We developed an empirical model to predict NUV-r vs. mass relationships and applied it to our data. It shows excellent match (>80%) with our observations across all mass ranges, except for a small discrepancy at lower mass levels.

Using this model, we forecast future observations from Legacy Survey, DESI, and PFS with high accuracy (>80%). Additionally, we used our model to identify extragalactic objects with unusual NUV-r vs. mass profiles. It led to the classification of ultra-distant galaxies such as DNB-19137773, DNb-10133726, DNb-10083016, DNb-10083017, and DNb-10133725 which lie off the predicted color-mass curve.
