Transfer learning has become a widely adopted approach for machine learning in languages other than English. A commonly used strategy involves fine-tuning a pretrained English model on the target language using parallel corpora. However, building datasets for parallel corpora can be challenging and expensive in certain languages. This paper challenges the conventional approach, claiming it's possible to leverage a pretrained English model to learn a sentiment classifier for languages without parallel corpora. We test this idea on Spanish and Chinese datasets, obtaining surprising results. In both cases, the English-based model outperforms the conventional approach using domestic corpora. In the evaluation of Spanish datasets, fine-tuning a bilingual dictionary proves as effective as using parallel corpora. In the evaluation of Chinese datasets, using domestic corpora alone surpasses the conventional approach. This breakthrough offers multiple contributions to the field, including (1) exploring the application of transfer learning in languages without parallel corpora, (2) discovering the feasibility of using bilingual dictionaries for fine-tuning, and (3) developing a novel approach to counter linguistic biases. This research provides insights into the boundaries and possibilities of cross-lingual machine learning. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/ghoulery/cross-lunar. The paper has been accepted for presentation at EMNLP 2022.

This paper introduces a novel verification approach and algorithm to ensure the correctness of programs modifying cache coherence protocols, specifically focusing on protocols like SCYSC and CPT. Unlike existing techniques, this method can automatically generate the smallest number of fence insertions required to prevent non-blocking data races from emerging. The proposed approach is part of a larger theory on verifying and correcting cache coherence protocols and can be applied to a broad category of lockless algorithms meeting certain specifications. The algorithm leverages the SCYNF framework, which facilitates both verification and correction of programs under certain protocol limitations. The algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through successful applications to SCYSC, CPT, and other protocols. The algorithm's fence insertion generation strategy is also an optimization problem with polynomial-time complexity. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against actual program behaviors, including simulations showing its effectiveness. The algorithm has been implemented as software tools usable for program verification and correction. The software, including the SCYNF framework, fence insertion generator, and protocols verified with the method, is available as an open-source repository. The software tools are part of a larger research effort but have been developed with practical applications in mind. The algorithms' performance is evaluated on various multi-core processors and cache configurations. The software has been evaluated on multiple research cases, including the CPT protocol on up to 16 cores and various cache settings. The software tools are available for download and can be used for both research and practical purposes. The algorithms have been found to be highly efficient, with verification and correction times typically measured in seconds despite the complexity of the algorithms. The study explores chaotic behavior in semiclassical mechanics through the Hénon-Heiles model, focusing on analyzing eigenvalue averages for actions corresponding to ground states and their classical counterparts. By examining classical action values at quantum action sheets, the investigation reveals the connection between quantum eigenvalue averages and classical behavior. Specifically, in the true minimum state scenario, the research finds that quantum eigenvalue averages mirror classical behavior for larger values. However, in the over shooting scenario, where the classical trajectory leaves the true minimum, the relationship between quantum eigenvalue averages and classical behavior becomes more complex, revealing a distinction between homoclinic orbits and double well orbits. The analysis also reveals a periodic pattern in the difference between quantum eigenvalue averages and classical behavior in the true minimum state scenario, in addition to identifying the impact of symmetry on this pattern. The findings are further confirmed through numerical simulations. The study concludes by highlighting the broader implications of these results for understanding chaotic behavior in semiclassical mechanics. Recently, high-performance models have been applied to Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), but these models face significant challenges during optimization due to limited and imbalanced annotation data. To address this issue, we propose a novel sampling approach called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS) that adapts the negative proposal sampling process to achieve more efficient optimization. By dividing proposals into sub-groups based on previously detected relationships and sampling negative proposals separately for each group, BNPS reduces the influence of irrelevant proposals and focuses learning on more critical annotation data. Our method incorporates two key components: 1) Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS) that adapts the negative proposal sampling process to achieve more efficient optimization, and 2) Progressive BNPS (PNPS) that addresses annotation imbalances by detecting relationships in multiple stages. Our research demonstrates that BNPS and PNPS significantly enhance the performance of VRD models by efficiently learning from limited and imbalanced annotation data. Compared to conventional sampling approaches, BNPS leads to a 2.3% improvement in mean Average Precision (mAP) for extractions and a 6.2% improvement in mAP for proposals. Moreover, PNPS leads to an additional 3.8% improvement in mAP for extractions. Our progressive approach also surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, such as End-to-End Visual Relationship Detection, by achieving a 39.8% mAP score for proposals and a 16.2% mAP score for extractions on the Visual Relationship Detection human-centric dataset, respectively. Our code and models are available for download at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/EVCR. Our research demonstrates that Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling and Progressive BNPS can be applied to other object detection tasks to tackle annotation imbalances.

We compared the performance of linear and nonlinear models in a controlled action recognition setting, varying the size of the training dataset from 300 to 3000 images representing 25 actions. Our findings showed that both models achieved similar results across different dataset sizes, with errors around 10% across all experiments. This suggests that either model can effectively handle the complexities of action recognition with minimal overfitting, even when trained on relatively small datasets. Notably, when trained on 3000 images, both models saw no improvement in performance despite increasing the training iterations by a factor of 10. This led us to conclude that neither model was benefiting from additional training, suggesting that the capacity of neither model was fully utilized in the smaller dataset iterations. To further explore this, we trained the models on a single dataset size of 3000 images with different data augmentation techniques, discovering that nonlinear models exhibited a notable decrease in errors with augmentation, while linear models showed little change. This prompted us to investigate the effectiveness of using action recognition APIs as a potential means of enriching the training data. Using one such API, we successfully reduced the error rate from 14.8% to 8.3%. Additionally, we discovered that the API's predictions, though inaccurate on their own, could be accurate enough to be incorporated into the training data, allowing us to recognize actions in new images. Ultimately, we were able to achieve the best results with a linear model, incorporating the API's predictions into the training data using a specific technique, thereby significantly improving the model's performance. Our method may provide a foundation for enhancing supervised action recognition models by leveraging these types of APIs.

Ultimately, this study proposes applicable scenarios for the machine in image processing and acknowledges the potential for a more efficient architecture utilizing four instead of eight bits per memory address. This could be achieved through the integration of additional memory modules. A well-trained neural model can effectively generate programs on its own, but it typically falls short when confronted with errors common in applications, such as those arising from invalid input causing a program to crash. To overcome this limitation, it's beneficial to incorporate guidance from a static program analyzer to identify potential issues and provide necessary corrections. However, building such a learning framework from scratch is a complex task. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages weak supervision from the analyzer to improve a neural program generator, enabling the model to learn from corrective feedback even when free to explore the program space. Experiments using the Python interpreter's static analyzer and the Jupyter notebook's kernel showed that this approach successfully induces the model to avoid crashes and generate functional programs, even when an ideal solver is not available. Notably, the model's performance was boosted by incorporating static analyzer guidance, achieving a 97% crash prevention rate in free exploration and 75% program correctness in constrained generation, compared to the baseline's 10% crash prevention rate in free exploration and 20% correctness in constrained generation. This method's ability to induce program correctness through weak supervision from the analyzer is a key contribution of this research. This technique can be applied to induce other program properties, such as security, by utilizing a different analyzer. This approach also facilitates the development of program generators that can evolve over time, as changes to the generator can be evaluated for their effectiveness by monitoring program property improvements. This is particularly relevant in domains where programs must evolve to remain functional and where inducing program property is a persistent goal. This approach is also compatible with program generator architectures that utilize multiple models, such as those employed in code completers. A extraordinarily large solar flare occurred on November 7th, 2004, which was both a X17-classima flare and the most powerful solar flare recorded in the history of space observations up to that point. This extraordinary event led to a rush to observe the associated X-ray source, solar particle storm, and Earth-directed solar radiation from space-based, airborne, and ground-based platforms. Although the proximity of the Galician spacecraft launch prevented in-flight testing of its solar flare sensor, the opportunity to test this device did arise when it passed through the relativistic solar wind some weeks later. Post-flight analysis of in-flight data revealed results that validated the initial theoretical predictions about the behavior of high-energy particles during solar flares. Furthermore, this experience provided valuable training and operational procedures for future space missions. Additionally, it led to the development of a more sophisticated model for predicting in-flight relativistic solar wind encounters. In the context of future deep space missions, this model is expected to play a crucial role in ensuring the effectiveness and reliability of in-flight scientific instruments. The lessons learned from this experience are expected to benefit not only the Galician spacecraft but also other interplanetary spacecraft. The relativistic fluid dynamics theory, specifically for scalar and vector mesons, has been repeatedly examined in various contexts, resulting in divergent findings that have not been comprehensively evaluated previously. This study surveys the different approaches to viscous relativistic fluid dynamics, focusing on the properties of scalar and vector mesons within the framework of linear response theory. We pinpoint the underlying assumptions that lead to distinct results and systematically compare the obtained dispersion relations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the correspondence between kinetic theory and holographic gravity in five dimensions, establishing a new understanding of meson behavior. The study also reveals that the dissipation of scalar and vector mesons follows distinct relaxation patterns, with the former exhibiting faster equilibration and the latter slower equilibration. Additionally, we derive low momentum meson dispersion relations and find that the scalar and vector meson thermodynamics are connected by a common chemical potential at zero momentum. These findings have significant implications for improving the simulation of scalar and vector mesons within relativistic fluid dynamics. Finally, we incorporate these developments into the Elucidate code suite and present results for the viscous scalar and vector meson diffusion coefficients. Lastly, we apply these modifications to simulate the LHC's StriFe experiment, with the outcome matching the available data. In the future, we intend to integrate these coefficients into Elucidate by utilizing the second-order gradient expansion of relativistic fluid dynamics. This advancement will enable the simulation of spontaneous symmetry breaking processes involving scalar and vector mesons. Nonetheless, our current implementation allows for the simulation of the Little Bang produced by the StriFe experiment. In this simulation, the temperature and chemical potential of the medium are raised abruptly, triggering the emission of scalar and vector mesons as a result of the created chemical potential within these particles. The emitted mesons are then detected and analyzed to produce spectra analogous to those obtained from actual particle detection processes. By adjusting the underlying assumptions of the simulation, distinct theoretical approaches can be evaluated, even those that surpass the second-order gradient expansion by incorporating more intricate kinetic theory aspects. Deep learning models have reached near-perfect levels in image recognition tasks like object detection and classification, yet their reliability is frequently called into question due to the lack of transparency in their decision-making process. This difficulty in understanding the models' behavior motivates the development of xAI (explanable artificial intelligence), a critical component that can showcase the working of these neural networks, thus ensuring their effectiveness. In this research paper, a novel xAI approach called Feature Importance Masking is presented, incorporating a new interpretation technique called Linear Visual Translation (LVT) for the existing ScoreCAM method. LVT is capable of providing insights into how the models' predictions are affected by specific input features. This new approach is applied to multiple detection and classification tasks, using multiple backends, and the results demonstrate that Feature Importance Masking provides the most accurate and consistent results compared to other methods, including the original ScoreCAM LVT implementation. For example, in the Cityscapes dataset, this approach yields accurate scores for the presence or absence of certain objects in scenes, such as cars (AUC-ROC: 0.9372) and bicycles (AUC-ROC: 0.9285). Furthermore, in real-world applications, this method has shown potential, as seen in demonstrations involving self-driving radar data and medical imaging. Although the proposed method has limitations, such as an increased computational requirement and a focus on convolutional neural networks, it offers a valuable starting point for developing more effective xAI techniques that can be adapted to a broader range of neural network architectures. Inciting users to spread false information and hacking social media platforms through fake accounts are common tactics used by malicious actors to disseminate false information and influence public opinion on Twitter. Unlike existing detection tools that focus solely on identifying and counteracting these threats, our innovative MetaFEND framework is designed to proactively prevent these attacks from spreading by identifying potential propaganda campaigns and fake accounts in advance. By integrating multiple models, MetaFEND combines logical rules with logical deductive reasoning to analyze relationships and underlying motivations behind users' actions and postings. By incorporating a synthetic data generator, MetaFEND can create diverse fake account profiles to simulate the behavior of these accounts in a realistic manner. In our experiments, we demonstrated that by utilizing both real and artificially created data, MetaFEND exhibited exceptional performance in distinguishing between genuine and fake accounts. Our findings revealed that the combinations of both types of data significantly improved the accuracy of detection models, with gains of up to 10% when using artificial data in addition to real data, according to our metrics. In particular, our research showed that MetaFEND's hybrid approach yielded outstanding results with gradient boosting models, achieving an F1 score of 0.879 in comparing model variations, which significantly outperformed the existing state-of-the-art model by achieving an F1 score of 0.779. Moreover, our research addressed the concern of privacy protection by implementing an anonymous data access protocol in collaboration with Twitter, ensuring that metadata associated with account and posting data was encrypted. In summary, our innovative MetaFEND framework represents a groundbreaking advancement in proactively preventing the spread of false information and hacking on Twitter. Consequently, we believe that our discoveries and techniques can serve as a model for addressing comparable challenges in other social media platforms. In addition, the skills and expertise developed in crafting this project can be applied to various other machine learning projects. We introduce a novel framework to establish connections between the probabilistic analysis of dynamical systems and their learning from time series data. By leveraging flux balance analysis, we represent complex systems as stochastic difference equations and apply state estimation to teach these systems new behaviors using observed data. We prove that under certain conditions, our method effectively learns the underlying structure of a new system instance. Additionally, we demonstrate the performance of this learning approach through simulations of a metabolic network and a macroeconomic model. Furthermore, we show that our technique can be an efficient alternative to model reduction techniques by comparing it with existing methods. We also investigate the implications of our approach on optimizing system performance and weigh the benefits and drawbacks of utilizing in silico data within the learning framework. Finally, we outline potential applications and future directions for this research. We have made our algorithm publicly available on a GitHub repository.

Advanced computer algorithms, in particular Deep Learning methods, have enhanced region detection and image segmentation performance. A key contributing factor to this improvement is the extensive training required for a Deep Learning model, which necessitates access to a vast portfolio of annotated images. Despite the initial success, several challenges persist, not least the time-consuming nature of annotating images for use in training. To mitigate this issue, a novel approach has been proposed, utilizing a limited set of annotated images in a specific region of interest, with the goal of training a convolutional neural network. A complementary technique, known as contrast enhancement, is incorporated to improve region detection accuracy. A range of region shapes and sizes are used in annotation, alongside multiple contrast enhancement approaches, to evaluate the effectiveness of this method. Experimental results using MRI datasets from the Osteochondromas Challenge 2018 and the Brain/Mind Challenge 2019 demonstrate significant gains in region of interest segmentation precision, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art. As massive spectroscopic surveys advance, collecting astrobot trajectories while maintaining safety and efficiency becomes increasingly complex. To tackle this challenge, we've developed an optimization framework that leverages a two-layer planning approach. In the inner layer, a constraint satisfaction problem ensures astrobots maintain a minimum safety distance from each other and from target observation areas. The outer layer, an mixed-integer linear programming problem, oversees trajectory coordination and scheduling while prioritizing efficiency. By dividing tasks into manageable subsets and solving a limited number of linear programming problems, our approach significantly reduces computational demands. We've tested this framework using real-world data and observed a substantial improvement in performance while achieving comparable results to industry standards. Moreover, our proposed method allows the seamless integration of both types of data, enriching the learning process and producing superior results in comparison to baseline models. Our experiments demonstrate notable enhancements in question-answering performance on the LCST dataset, achieving a 45.3% score for the low-resource setting and a 51.3% score for the medium-resource setting. A comprehensive theoretical framework is introduced to explain the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes (SMBHs) within the context of an expanding universe. This framework incorporates observations of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and builds upon the standard model of SMBH growth through mergers. It includes AGN-driven outflows, fueling, and mass transmissions from SMBHs to galaxies' stellar and gas components. By incorporating these processes, our model reveals a self-regulating loop between SMBHs and their host galaxies. Here, the interplay between outflows and fueling leads to the stabilization of a bimodal state. This state is characterized by a steady SMBH growth phase, separated from an outflow-dominated phase. The latter is a transient phenomenon. The transient nature of the outflow-dominated phase is accountable for the observations of AGNs with outflows. The duration of these observations is governed by the mass of the galaxy's central bulge. The presence of outflows in our universe is confirmed through a parameter-free prediction related to hard X-ray spectra. The most striking outcome, however, is the prediction that galaxy mergers trigger the onset of outflows, thereby facilitating SMBH growth within an evolving universe. The most suitable observational platform for testing these predictions is the combination of future wide-field hard X-ray missions, such as the Effective Aperture X-ray Telescope Array and the Enhanced X-ray Imaging Mission. The proposed framework also addresses the diversity of galaxy spectra, revealing a link between absorption patterns and the presence of outflows, and providing a theoretical basis for studying the cosmic evolution of SMBHs and their host galaxies. The implementation of this framework within a supermassive BBH numerical relativity code is also described. The code is now capable of tracking the behavior of SMBHs within their host galaxies' contexts, offering new insights into the properties of gravitational waves generated by these systems. The development of this code leads to predictions related to first-generation gravitational wave events, such as those observable signals that could be mimicked by variable hard X-ray sources from galaxies' centers. The framework is also applicable to studying the impact of AGNs on the surrounding gas and their potential effects on the cosmic reionization process. The code is available upon request from the corresponding author. The findings presented in this study are the outcome of collaborations with S. K. Yajima, T. Tanaka, and K. Nakajima. A novel Multi-Band Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (MBDPCRN) approach has been developed for speech enhancement. This model builds upon the established Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) framework, which improves speech quality by leveraging time-frequency domain information and reducing over-reliance on model parameters. The Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) architecture, despite achieving high performance, is limited by the large number of parameters required. To mitigate this, the proposed MBDPCRN model splits the frequency spectrum into multiple bands, allowing each band to be processed by a separate, compact DPCRN component. This strategy significantly reduces the number of model parameters while maintaining excellent speech enhancement performance. The MBDPCRN model offers an efficient alternative for speech enhancement, with notable implications for real-time audio applications. Experimental evaluations conducted on public datasets reveal that the MBDPCRN model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially fewer parameters. Moreover, the model's efficiency enables seamless deployment on mobile devices. Furthermore, the introduction of the MBDPCRN architecture paves the way for exploring more advanced multi-band convolution recurrent networks in speech and other sequence-based processing areas. The authors have made their model publicly available to facilitate replication and advancement of this research. Speech enhancement results achieved with the MBDPCRN model have been consistently superior, with an average spectral distortion of 1.53, outperforming traditional deep learning methods and competing models, including the baseline DPCRN architecture with 1.76 SD. The authors have also released the protocol for replicating the experiments conducted in this study, including model training and testing, at the following address: https://github.com/ghulame/MBDPCRN/tree/main/Replicating_Results. The authors hope that sharing this code will facilitate replication and encourage further innovation within this area of research. These tests, which involve comparing the turn-around radii of secondary and primary objects in a given population, are statistically independent of existing methods based on mass ratios. A theoretical framework for analyzing systematic errors in this type of test is also presented. When considering uncertainties in mass-to-light ratios and the range of satellite galaxies' eccentricities, we find that the results are robust enough to provide a useful constraint on the dark matter density parameter Omega_d > 0.045 (95% C.I.). When combined with existing constraints based on mass ratios, this new limit further reduces the allowable parameter space by about a factor of two. To enhance the sensitivity of its experiments at the LHC, the CMS collaboration upgraded its detector system with advanced technology. The previous pixel detector, introduced in 2010, underwent significant upgrades to boost its data collection capabilities. Although it initially functioned effectively, it became clear that the detector required upgraded readout electronics and a new system to manage data loss. Consequently, a 4000-newton cm negative magnetic field was applied to improve track finding, resulting in the installation of a new diamond detector system called the Beam Pick-up Detectors (BPUD). However, the primary upgrade involved the introduction of a new silicon pixel detector, featuring an increased active material area of 4 x 4 cm squared and 80 million processing channels. This new detector, incorporating a readout architecture known as the Particle Flow Pixel Readout Challenge (PFPRC), was designed to enhance data collection speed and reduce parasitic currents. A new optical link system based on 40-Gbit/s serial links was also developed to manage 10.12 Tbit/s of data. To validate its performance, the new detector underwent comprehensive testing, including magnetized beam and cosmic ray probes, ultimately demonstrating its capability to collect up to 12.5 gigapixels per second and 10.12 Tbit/s of data. This breakthrough technology has been in operation since 2016 with notable achievements including the discovery of the Higgs boson and advances in top quark studies, lepton pair production, and vector boson scattering. As the LHC enters its phase II, the upgraded pixel detector remains committed to delivering exceptional performance with improved readout technology and increased data collection capabilities. To build on this success, R\&D for future detectors is already underway with the introduction of highly integrated digital pixel detectors featuring in-pixel digital signal processing. This represents a significant evolution in pixel detector technology and is expected to play a crucial role in the detection systems for future colliders and experimental research. The success of data-driven dialogue systems heavily relies on their ability to generalize beyond training conversations. We suggest that maintaining a clear focus and producing relevant dialogue can be achieved through role specifications, which guide the system using context and character descriptions. We showcase the value of role specifications in polished, natural conversations and demonstrate that incorporating them enhances the system's performance. Additionally, we find that specifying roles through context proves more effective than a more explicit approach, and this methodology can be versatile in its implementation and data utilization. The system's effectiveness is further highlighted by our tests in both single-turn and multi-turn dialogues. A system built on this principle has been made publicly available. We also introduce a simple method for generating role descriptions in context, which produces natural and coherent output. This methodology represents a foundational step in creating data-driven dialogue systems that can engage in focused and relevant conversations. Immersive videos offer an engaging, first-person perspective but pose a challenge due to their atypical viewing path. Recent advancements in viewport prediction have shown potential, with many models relying on additional information such as video subtitles. However, the high production cost and cultural limitations of subtitles restrict their widespread use. To address this constraint, we investigate whether video subtitles are indeed necessary for accurate viewport prediction. Our findings reveal that, surprisingly, subtitles have a limited impact on prediction accuracy and that models can perform well without them. To further explore this discovery, we developed a new dataset without audio-visual data, using only the text in subtitles, to test the efficacy of zero-shot learning approaches. Our experiments demonstrate that these methods can effectively predict viewports without audio-visual data, but with lower accuracy than models using video. To facilitate progress in this area, we released the new dataset along with a baseline model incorporating these constraints. This initiative aims to pave the way for developing immersive video viewports without relying on extensive, expensive-to-produce video data. By creating a higher-level system of unitary operators that approximate the time evolution and thermal states of a original system, we reduce the bond dimension requirement from $D \sim L^d$ to $D \sim d \log L$ for large L. Approximately solving the Hamiltonian's time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger equation is also achievable using this approach. A specific example is applied to quantum spin chains. This method effectively lessens the computational burden associated with implementing lattice-scale quantum thermal dynamics. A separate observation made in our study is that even small systems can exhibit non-thermal behavior when subjected to time-varying conditions. A new unitary operator hierarchy is introduced that enforces decreasing entropy along its progression, simulating the cooling effect often seen in closed systems over time. A concrete model is utilized to demonstrate these concepts. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum thermal dynamics, especially how entropy behavior in isolated systems can emulate the cooling process, and how a novel PEPO framework can generate thermal states and time-evolution approximations with reduced bond dimension requirements that scale with system size, ultimately holding implications for the development of lattice-scale quantum thermal dynamics simulations. A concrete model also highlights the unitary operator hierarchy's entropy-reducing effect. This paper builds upon previous research of the authors with N. Nguyen, addressing the long-standing challenge of determining optimal decoupling values for polynomials with irreducible factors. To overcome this difficulty, the authors employ a combined strategy of Taylor series analysis and canonical surfaces to achieve significant insights into the behavior of polynomials near their critical points. Theoretical results obtained using this approach are validated through numerical computations using MATLAB. The authors present several novel theorems to illustrate the efficacy of their method, especially for polynomials defined by rational functions and those with non-smooth critical points. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that their approach allows for the identification of critical points in polynomial systems that cannot be solved using traditional methods from computational algebra. The algorithms developed as part of this research are efficient in terms of memory usage, even for massive data sets, as demonstrated by an accompanying paper presenting numerical results for over one thousand parameter values for a renowned model problem in chemistry. That model problem is particularly notorious for its extremely small decoupling values which are difficult to determine either numerically or analytically. That research has been recognized by the award of a prize from the Jacques Herbrand award committee in 2019. The authors are eager to share their method with experts in the field, provide computational tools, and encourage them to contribute their own research and insights for further collaboration. That collaboration will take place within the framework of the recently established nonstandard analysis network where researchers are working together to advance the understanding of real analysis and its applications in mathematics and elsewhere. The authors hope that this initiative will give rise to new perspectives and a broader view of the subject, its history, and its future. This study introduces a new capacity metric called anisotropic capacity and establishes connections to existing capacity frameworks, including the Poisson capacity, anisotropic Poisson capacity, and spherical capacity. Anisotropic capacity is shown to be equivalent to the anisotropic logarithmic capacity and a recent definition involving the anisotropic capacity of a domain has a direct relationship with the anisotropic capacity of its complement. Furthermore, the relationship between anisotropic capacity and Eicholf's logarithmic capacity formula has been established, leading to new results for (p,q)-systems and Muckenhoupt weights. Additionally, the paper proves that anisotropic capacity is p-arithmetic and explores its connection to geometric inequalities, including modified Fefferman inequality and a recent volumetric inequality by Tysk. The relationship between anisotropic capacity and singular integrals with non-smooth kernels has also been investigated. The paper concludes with an exploration of its methods' applicability to establish (p,q)-system inequalities. To achieve this, we demonstrated that even determining whether one strong shortest path exists between two nodes in a weighted graph is an NP-complete problem. Additionally, we found that approximating the k-strong shortest path union cover problem is NP-hard. However, we developed a brute force method with a high computational complexity of O(n^3 * 2^n) to solve the k-strong shortest path union cover problem efficiently for small input sizes. Furthermore, we defined an optimal solution based on minimum weight k-strong shortest paths and proposed a method with a computational complexity of O(n^3 * n^k) that determines the optimal k-strong shortest path union cover. However, this method is practical only for small values of n. To handle larger input sizes, we proposed two approximate algorithms. In this study, a novel type of magnetophotonic crystal is analyzed, made from a thin layer of gold placed above a glycerin substrate and surrounded by air. When irradiated with light, a particular wavelength exhibits significant variation in both refractive index and polarization. The origin of this phenomenon lies in the interaction between surface plasmons and Rayleigh anomalies, which create an optical resonance. The arrangement of this system is modified to rotate the crystal by 45 degrees, resulting in an abrupt change in optical properties at a specific wavelength. The associated spectral patterns can be understood through the combination of surface plasmon and Rayleigh anomaly optical resonances, and their relationship with magnetophotonic crystals is established through proper design parameters. Experimental evidence confirms the theoretical findings, and the constructed device is capable of detecting magnetic fields through a significant shift in the optical transition at approximately 531 nanometers. This detection capability is anticipated to operate over a broader spectral range if the design is modified to accommodate multiple wavelength signals. The proposed system provides a foundation for the development of magnetic field-sensitive devices and could pave the way for advanced applications in magnetophotonic technology. Theoretical modeling is validated through experimental data from a fabricated prototype. The design is optimized to function at specific wavelengths, and the associated spectral patterns can be controlled through proper design parameters. The resulting device is capable of detecting magnetic fields based on optical properties and could be expanded to handle multiple wavelength signals. The concept may lead to innovative uses for magnetophotonic crystals. In recent years, knowledge distillation has proven an effective method for black-box model compression. A new approach called decision-based black-box knowledge distillation assumes that the teacher model's labeling process involves making decisions based on the input, without accessing the internal model architecture or weights. This approach assumes a significant psychological aspect, reflecting how humans might learn from each other's decisions, rather than relying on the original data. It claims that a student model can learn from a teacher model by minimizing the discrepancy between their decision outcomes, given the same input. This perspective offers an alternative to conventional knowledge distillation methods, which focus on leveraging the teacher model's probability distributions to update the student model. To evaluate DB3, we compare its performance to conventional knowledge distillation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Kinetics datasets, using ResNet50, MobileNetV2, and RFB, and find that DB3 can achieve similar or better performance than conventional knowledge distillation. Additionally, DB3 is more robust to label noise, outperforming conventional knowledge distillation when the teacher model is soft-labeling. This indicates that decision-based black-box knowledge distillation is a reliable and robust compression method for computer vision models. The paper updates the previous measurements made by BaBar of the branching fractions $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$, as well as investigates $B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0$ decays in a mass range extending to 18.46 GeV in units of $\sqrt{s}$. The research is based on 468 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at 7 TeV and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The new results are: for $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$, the relative uncertainty is enhanced to 7.5%; for $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$, the uncertainty remains nearly unchanged at 13.1%; and in the mass range extension, the detection of an excess of events around 8 GeV in units of $\sqrt{s}$ is reported, consistent with previous BaBar findings. No significant peaks aside from $B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0$ and $B^0_s \to D_s^{-} J/ψ J/ψ$ are found in this extended mass range. The research results in a more precise branching fraction measurement for $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$, but the determination of $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$ remains less accurate due to systematic uncertainties associated with $B^0$ decay mode calculations. The findings also reduce the discrepancy between BaBar and LHCb's previous measurements of $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to D_s^{-} K_S^0)$. Though the research provides evidence for an excess of events in the mass range extension, further study is needed to identify the underlying cause for this phenomenon. Upcoming experiments with increased luminosity and more sophisticated detection systems at the LHC will likely significantly improve the understanding of these rare decay modes. Until then, BaBar's findings in this area will remain a significant contribution to the field. The full dataset at both 7 TeV and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies is utilized in this research

Given a multiplicity-free module, its submodule lattice can be reconstructed using its composition factors and branch coefficients derived from the irreducible constituents of a contragredient module. Here, we extend this process to any module with a multiplicity-free quotient, determining the necessary parameters to reconstruct its lattice from the composition factors of the quotient and additional data related to the branch coefficients of the contragredient module. A key aspect involves defining a weighted partition of the composition factors based on the branch coefficients of the contragredient module. Specifically, for a multiplicity-free module $\mathfrak{m}$, we establish a bijection between the set of weighted partitions of $\mathfrak{m}$ and the lattice $\Gamma(\mathfrak{m}^{\vee})$, yielding a natural order on weighted partitions. Moreover, the maximum weighted partition corresponds to the highest weight vertex in the branch graph $\Gamma(\mathfrak{m}^{\vee})$. This framework also enables the analysis of filtered modules and their extension functors. For self-dual modules $\mathfrak{m}$ with positive weight, we examine the relationship between weighted partitions and the structure of $\Gamma(\mathfrak{m})$. Finally, we provide examples illustrating the construction of weighted partitions in various scenarios.

The Strong Geodetic Recognition problem can be defined as identifying whether a given graph G and a specific vertex set S contain a unique geodetic subset within S. This research extends the investigation of the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem to graph classes that include cubic graphs, planar graphs, and line graphs. Specifically, we explore the strength of polynomial-time decisionability for this problem in instances where a graph G and a vertex set S are provided, with the additional condition that S is a strong geodetic subset of G. Our findings reveal that determining whether a graph class contains a unique geodetic subset is generally NP-complete, except in instances where the graph class is cubic, planar, line, or series-parallel, in which case the ability to make this determination is achieved through tractable methods. Moreover, we examine the strength of polynomial-time decisionability for identifying a minimum strong geodetic subset within a given graph G and vertex set S, with or without the additional condition that S is a strong geodetic subset of G. Our results demonstrate that determining a minimum strong geodetic subset in instances where S is not necessarily strong geodetic of G is generally NP-hard, except in instances where the graph class is cubic, planar, line, or series-parallel, in which case the ability to do so is achieved through tractable methods, with an added condition that when S is cubic or planar, the ability to do so is achieved through tractable methods without restrictions. Even with the most advanced algorithms, imitation learning still struggles to achieve optimal results due to its reliance on perfectly designed demonstration samples. This issue is addressed by the TRAIL framework, which discovers relevant but suboptimal data by playing an online game against a virtual partner. This additional data is then used to refine the policy through corrected value functions. The key benefit of TRAIL is its improved sample efficiency, surpassing traditional imitation learning methods when the teacher is highly reliable. When the teacher makes errors, the TRAIL framework effectively identifies and eliminates noise. Furthermore, the TRAIL framework can be paired with any offline learning algorithm by treating the demonstrations as special cases of irrelevant data. The theoretical foundations of TRAIL are rooted in online learning, online imitation learning, and matrix updates. The code for the TRAIL framework is openly available, demonstrating its superior performance in complex tasks involving navigation and first-person manipulation. The TRAIL framework offers a versatile solution to enhance self-improvement and online learning, making it suitable for a broad range of applications. Co-learning with peers and experts is a well-established technique, notably effective in reinforcement learning, where expert guidance is often limited due to the high cost of obtaining expert demonstrations. Our work proposes a novel approach, Co-Imitation Learning, which leverages fellow learners' suboptimal performance to accelerate learning from limited expert feedback. We demonstrate that fellow learners can significantly contribute to learning, especially in scenarios where they have access to more abundant experience data. Building on this finding, we develop an efficient algorithm for Co-Imitation Learning, combining expert policy imitation and self-imitation, supported by theoretical convergence guarantees. Experimental results show that our method outperforms baseline algorithms in various environments, including video games and robotic tasks, with impressive improvements facilitated by the exchange of learning data with fellow agents. Notably, this cooperation enables learning from as little as one expert demonstration. The code for our method is openly available at https://github.com/awhaofeng/Co-Imitation-Learning. Our work provides a new perspective on imitation learning within cooperative co-learning settings and paves the way for further exploration in collaborative multi-agent learning scenarios. Ultimately, Cooperative Imitation Learning may help unlock more efficient and effective learning from both human and agent teachers. Nonetheless, these approaches often depend on the action space being identical in size to the vocabulary, thus requiring the removal of unnecessary action options to maximize effectiveness. We contend that, instead of reducing the action space size, it's more beneficial to directly optimize actions for high quality. In our research, we propose an approach to declare desired properties for actions that capture complex rewards. Moreover, we show that strict conditions are met for the expressiveness of our neural data rewards model. Moreover, experimental results reveal significant performance improvements over current state-of-the-art approaches across three evaluation metrics for the large vocabulary English-to-Chinese and English-to-Japanese machine translation tasks. Additionally, our method is found to outperform the baseline in low-resource settings with a smaller action space. We have made the data and code available for replication purposes. Our novel reward model has a high level of expressiveness and can be viewed as a neural version of the data-driven reward model. It's also the first time that combining external knowledge in reinforcement learning for neural machine translation has been proposed. Establishing accurate end-effector pose estimates is crucial in robotics and is often achieved through a process called calibration. A team of researchers suggested utilizing machine learning to enhance the robustness of this estimation by incorporating additional sensory input from a camera positioned at various distances. They demonstrated that using a depth camera significantly improves the performance of their model, especially when it's placed farther away, and revealed that a particular configuration, where the camera is placed at a distance equal to the end-effector from the base of the robotic arm, yields the most optimal results. Through simulation and practical applications, they proved that their proposed method not only increases the robustness of their model but also allows it to handle changes in its environment. A key finding showed that using a depth camera from a closer distance can lead to overfitting, which can be avoided when it's positioned at a greater distance. Additionally, they found that using a depth camera instead of a regular one doesn't significantly impact the model's performance. To train their model, they used a process called reinforcement learning, which involves training multiple machines simultaneously to mimic the varying conditions that might be encountered during actual use. A key advantage of this approach is that it minimizes the need for human input during training. A practical application of this research was demonstrated through a calibration process used in a surgical robot, and results showed that the model performed at a high level even in complex environments. A key feature of this approach is its ability to handle unexpected changes, or "bailout" cases, where the estimated pose differs significantly from the actual position. A study of these bailout cases revealed that the model performs well in most instances, but can sometimes result in inaccurate estimates. A closer analysis of these instances revealed a pattern where the estimated pose could differ significantly from the actual position. A further investigation into this pattern led to a discovery where it was found that a particular configuration, where the camera is positioned at a distance equal to the end-effector from the base of the robotic arm, yields the most optimal results. A study of this pattern revealed that it follows a specific mathematical shape, and a key feature of this shape is that it represents a minimum point. A further analysis of this minimum point revealed that it represents a point of stability, and that any deviation from this point would result in an unstable situation. A key implication of this finding is that the model performs best when the camera is positioned at a distance equal to the end-effector from the base of the robotic arm. The Web's impact on the rise of political polarization requires assessment beyond economic and social effects, necessitating a deeper examination of how online influencers disseminate ideological views. We contend that Internet users' browsing habits, shaping their exposure to information, are a key factor in the spread of political ideology. We also argue that hyperlinks' influence on browsing habits is merely a layer superimposed upon the underlying web surfing dynamics, which drive the formation of ideological echo chambers. In contrast to the temporary nature of web surfers' connections, online communities' political affiliations endure. We demonstrate that web surfing habits' long-term patterns, emerging from infinite, random surfing, resemble the distribution of visit durations for online communities' websites, and also find corresponding similarities between web surfing habits and the distribution of votes cast between online communities' websites, especially those with shorter visit durations. Furthermore, we explore and counter potential methodological mistakes in prior research, and also examine the unstated assumptions underlying our approach, utilizing data from Wikipedia's election-based organization structure and voting records, and also data from Wikipedia's hyperlink network, Internet search engine traffic, and online news consumption patterns. We also develop a stochastic web surfing model, incorporating an infinite number of clickable links, to mathematically prove that the distribution of web surfing habits' bi-temporal patterns reflects the distribution of website visit durations, and also provide empirical evidence confirming the applicability of this model to a broad range of web surfing scenarios. We also determine the degree of websites' permanence within users' browsing history, and also find corresponding similarities between the distribution of web surfing habits' bi-temporal patterns, website visit durations, and the distribution of votes cast between online communities' websites. We now reverse this situation, using this context-free language to define V, and prove that any group that has the same presentation as V will have a similar property regarding context-free language. As a result, V is equivalent to a class of groups whose identity elements' context-free languages are deterministic and can be recognized in linear time. An open quantum system can exchange information with its environment, promoting two-way communication between the system and the surrounding space. This phenomenon of bidirectional information flow typically requires the system and environment to be linked by an interactive channel. In contrast, an open system that is not connected to a specific channel can seemingly only send information to its surrounding space, appearing to limit its ability to receive back information. This apparent restriction on bidirectional information flow can be overcome by taking a coarse-grained view of the environment, one that focuses on the correlations between parts of the environment rather than individual components. A simple example of this, involving a two-level system interacting with a collection of identical two-level systems, shows that when viewed through these coarse-grained lenses, the environment itself becomes an effective tool for receiving information from the system. This is in line with the principles of quantum metrology, which utilize the same type of environment. In this case, however, there is no need for the system and environment to be linked by an interactive channel. Instead, the relationships between different parts of the environment serve the purpose of receiving information about the system's state. In this way, bidirectional information flow can occur between the system and the environment without the need for an interactive channel that links them directly. This provides a new means of controlling the information flow between open systems and their surroundings. In particular, it could be used to improve the detection of phase shifts in quantum networks. In these applications, the focus is typically on certain specific parts of the environment, such as qubits between which the system and environment are interacting. This usually requires the system and environment to be linked by an interactive channel. In contrast, when viewed through these coarse-grained lenses, the environment itself can provide a different means of receiving information about the system, one that does not rely on this direct interaction but rather on the system's effect on the state of these specific parts of the environment. This new perspective on the environment as a means of receiving information about open systems offers opportunities for improving the precision of these applications without the need for direct interaction between the system and environment. We define an advanced form of finite state automata called p/q-automata that can recognize subsets of (N_p/q)^d, and we establish that any such acceptable set can also be recognised by a significantly simpler type of automaton called d-fold automata. This significant reduction in complexity of automata occurs when the indexing ratio p/q has a particularly straightforward form - namely when it is rational. Additionally, we can accurately characterize the subsets of (N_p/q)^d that can be recognised by finite state automata in terms of those recognisable by d-fold automata. This characterisation reveals a close relationship between these subsets and those recognisable by 1/fold automata, where f is the least common multiple of the denominators of all fractions in p/q. It is also demonstrated that any subset of (N_p/q)^d, which can be determined by a finite state automaton, can be seen as the union of subsets that can be recognised by 1/fold automata, for various values of f, and that this union is minimal and discrete. This study is an extension of prior research by Chlewicki and Schutzenberger, Ito, Berstien, Kitaev, Mal'cev, and others in the field of free groups and rational bases. It provides an overall framework that integrates these different theories and also offers new insights, particularly on the interconnection between automata theory, group theory, and number theory. It is also shown that this characterisation is optimal by constructing examples that demonstrate the capacity of p/q-automata to surpass that of d-fold automata. It is hoped that this research will contribute to a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationships between automata, groups, and numbers. This study focuses on a catalog of 33,619 binary candidates, derived from 24,453 multiple-spectrum entries, containing 26,985 optical linear spectroscopic binaries, 6,516 double-lined spectra suggesting 3,969 binary candidates other than spectroscopic binaries, and 715 near-infrared binary candidates. To extract radial velocity from multiple-spectrum entries, LAMOST's time-domain survey adopted the "template method," producing RVs from a total of 2,658,434 RV measurements for individual targets. Recent advancements in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have led to significant breakthroughs in image segmentation. Researchers have discovered an innovative approach called Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), incorporating edge-guided gate modules that refine predictions based on image edges. Inspired by EG-CNNs, we propose an alternative module called Point-Gated CNNs (PG-CNNs) that leverages local patterns to enhance model performance. In PG-CNNs, a dedicated module identifies distinct features at specific points, fusing them to improve segmentation accuracy. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the MS COCO and PASCAL-VRDD datasets demonstrate the efficacy of Point-Gated CNNs, showcasing superior results compared to EG-CNNs and the original network. The models' practical applications are also highlighted through examples of semantic mask refinement and object editing. The source code is publicly available on GitHub, contributing to the advancement of atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) module variants that have been publicly shared. Moreover, a comprehensive study comparing PG-CNNs to EG-CNNs, including code, is published on arXiv, facilitating further research in this area.

Specifically, it analyzes three MongoDB deployments, namely WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER, finding that they ensure variants of strong and weak isolation, respectively. By analyzing special cases, we demonstrate that the concept of e-positivity can be applied to specific functions while leaving other instances unaddressed. Notably, we establish the e-positivity of certain sums related to chromatic symmetric functions, particularly those associated with Dyck paths and Kimura numbers. The success of all-data performance is often hindered by implicit biases found in medical image datasets. These biases are embedded in the relationships between the input images and their corresponding clinical tags. As a result, models developed from these datasets tend to generalize poorly. To mitigate this limitation, we propose an approach that leverages unlabeled medical images to identify and disentangle the implicit biases present in datasets. By extracting the underlying noise from biases, we can generate debiased datasets that allow models to generalize effectively across different patient populations. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can generate diverse, bias-free datasets, leading to notable improvements in the accuracy of medical image analysis models in real-world scenarios. Specifically, we observe significant advancements in identifying lymph nodes in chest X-rays and classifying stroke types in CT scans, both with and without the presence of implicit biases. Moreover, we observe that the best-performing models in the tested scenarios achieve RoI-AUC scores of 0.8791 and 0.8339 for lymph node detection and stroke type classification, respectively. These outcomes underscore the value of addressing implicit biases in medical image datasets to achieve superior generalization. We have made our code and datasets available for public access.

We studied the effects of high pressure on Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$, a complex orthorhombic perovskite-related structure, using synchrotron radiation and X-ray diffraction at high pressures. Our experiments revealed that this material adapts to increasing pressure by increasing its lattice parameters, shifting to a tetragonal phase before ultimately stabilizing in the pseudocubic phase. These phase transitions occur at approximately 8 GPa and 15 GPa, respectively. Upon reaching the tetragonal phase, the material's volume decreases, while in the pseudocubic phase, the lattice volume increases, surpassing its initial volume at pressures exceeding 20 GPa. Notably, the material exhibits significant hardness, with a hardness increment of ~1 GPa per lattice parameter change, in alignment with global trends. Nonetheless, its hardening is largely attributed to the increased stability of the Ti$^{4+}$ oxidation state rather than any hardening associated with the Ti site itself. Interestingly, the electronic structure of this material shows an opposition between localized electrons at the Ti site and the delocalized electrons across the Bi site, which may influence its mechanical properties under pressure. Overall, this study highlights the value of combining structural and mechanical investigations with theoretical analysis of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under pressure to gain a more comprehensive understanding of its behavior.

A possible solution to address this limitation is to perform computations along multiple initial displacement paths before determining a final estimate of reachability and error bounds. A new theory posits that behind a strong shock wave, with an adiabatic index greater than a specific threshold, there emerges a singular region with an infinite density at the shock's origin. Contrary to this, observed patterns around central explosions suggest that densities should be finite. To investigate this discrepancy, the present model analyzes pressures and densities behind strong shocks, assuming they can be represented by power laws. It is discovered that when the adiabatic index exceeds a certain critical value, which is equal to three for planar and spherical shocks, but varies with density for orthogonal shocks, a singularity develops at the shock's origin, prompting the proposal of a modified adiabatic index that can be used in lieu of the original for analytical purposes. As an example, general relativistic orthogonal shocks with matter fields are examined, revealing that in these cases, the singularity can be avoided, and a finite density can exist at the shock's origin, consistent with the observed patterns of central explosions. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that in these situations, the modified adiabatic index is less than three, and its value can be determined through the conserved quantity theorem. Additionally, it is shown that when the big bang model is reinterpreted, with the initial condition of a finite density at the origin, it is possible to explain the distribution of matter densities across the universe. Finally, it is proposed that a similar mechanism could also apply to black hole formation. Leveraging this new framework, a specific shock wave solution is derived from a central explosion with an initial finite density, and its graphical representation is provided. It is observed that this type of shock wave pattern is distinct from the one generated by a singularity at the origin, and may be identifiable through astronomical observations. Lastly, it is suggested that this theory has implications for our understanding of the universe's earliest stages and the formation of black holes. However, further astronomical evidence is necessary to validate these hypotheses.

BART is a powerful neural language model with numerous applications, however its basic structure hinders its ability to generate correct word order. To address this issue, we propose using linearized trees (LTs) as a generative framework, specifically proposing LT-Generator, a BART-based model that generates words by constructing partial tree structures and ascending down them. We evaluate LT-Generator on the partial tree linearization (PTL) task from the Hackett and Shieber (2007) dataset, a related task to word ordering. Our results indicate that LT-Generator surpasses BART and other language models in PTL and matching tasks, and our analysis reveals the advantages of using linearized trees over baseline models. Additionally, we find that LT-Generator exhibits a local search strategy, often producing optimal or near-optimal outputs, in contrast to the tendency of other models to become stuck in local minima. We also observe a notable phenomenon where LT-Generator tends to generate words in the same order as the target words, and our interpretation suggests this as evidence for the model's generation process. To facilitate future research, we will make the code, data, and experiments openly accessible.

The creation and dissemination of deepfakes pose an emerging threat to both national security and societal stability. Deepfake detection methods have shown promise but are not without limitations, primarily due to their exclusive ability to operate with specific image modalities such as audio, video, or both. To address this constraint, this paper introduces MDNet-XSC, a pioneering deepfake detection framework that leverages cross-stitch connections to integrate knowledge across different domains. MDNet-XSC boasts an efficient architecture which allows it to effectively fuse multi-domain information by incorporating external side information through cross-stitch connections, thus enhancing the performance compared to conventional approaches. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the FFDataset and the NVIDIA Deepfake Challenge Dataset demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed MDNet-XSC in both single-shot and retraining scenarios, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models by achieving a notable improvement of 3.45% in overall accuracy. Moreover, the compact architecture of MDNet-XSC, enabled by code pruning, attains a remarkable 26.19% improvement in mean squared error (MSE) compared to the existing efficient model, improving the model's efficiency without compromising accuracy. The source code of the proposed model is openly available on GitHub.

Under the assumption of sub-Gaussian data, our analysis shows that DR-DSGD converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{K}+\lambda K^{-\beta N}\right)$ for non-concave functions and $\mathcal{O}\left(\lambda K^{-\beta N}\right)$ for concave functions, where $K$ is the number of iterations, $\lambda$ is the step size, and $\beta N$ represents the average degree of the network. What's more, our results demonstrate that DR-DSGD's performance can be optimized by adjusting the step size and the network topology. Compared to standard DSGD, DR-DSGD reduces the large communication burden of central nodes by allowing them to make larger steps, resulting in a significant acceleration of convergence. Our findings are verified by conducting numerical experiments on decentralized matrix factorization and extreme multi-maker learning. Notably, DR-DSGD outperforms standard DSGD and decentralized gradient descent in scenarios with large nodes. What's more, our results show that DR-DSGD can effectively mitigate the negative impact of unsynchronized updates in decentralized learning. Overall, DR-DSGD represents a fast-converging and efficient algorithm for decentralized learning that can be applied to a broad range of non-convex optimization problems. For nearly four decades, researchers have been intrigued by the complex scenario of a phase transition in hard-disk systems, particularly the challenging task of accurately identifying the behavior at this transition point. Recent observations involving highly energetic initial conditions have significantly complicated the picture, and it was suspected that these conditions led to a chaotic state almost instantaneously, making the existence of a coherent transition questionable. However, by analyzing the behavior of hard-disk systems through molecular dynamics simulations, this study finds that there is, in fact, a coherent transition, and it can be understood by looking at the development of a disordered state in smaller systems. Additionally, it was found that there is a clear distinction between two scenarios: a transition that occurs when the average initial separation between disks is greater than twice the diameter of a disk, and a more complex behavior at closer initial conditions. The former can be understood through a simple model that involves a disordered state developing over time, and it is proposed that this complexity at closer initial conditions is due to a non-equilibrium state of disk motion that is governed by a different rule than that observed in larger systems. The challenge of observing the transition in larger systems accurately is further highlighted by the variation of pressure measurements in simulations conducted with a medium-sized system, and by the need for extremely precise time and spatial steps in molecular dynamics simulations of smaller systems. The intricate nature of this transition, and the associated challenges it poses, make this problem an engaging problem for computational science. A pervasive issue in cryptocurrency is the prevalence of scams, with many victims losing significant amounts of money in pyramid schemes. Despite the sophistication of modern cryptocurrency analysis tools, there is a noticeable lack of empirical research focusing on the behavioral aspects of users in relation to fraudulent activities, including Forsage - a decentralized multi-level platform that has been identified as a pyramid scheme. To gain insight into user behavior and financial transactions within Forsage, we analyzed the public data available on the cryptocurrency exchange website CryptoStats, which provides detailed information on Forsage users and their earnings/losses. Our data shows that the majority of Forsage users suffer financial losses, with over 70% of users experiencing losses in the long term. We identified several key factors that influence users' ability to earn money in Forsage, including the level they are at within the network and the number of users they have recruited. Our research also reveals that users' earnings/losses in Forsage can be predicted using previous levels of earnings/losses, with a high degree of accuracy, indicating that the behavior of users in relation to Forsage is consistent and follows a pattern. To model this relationship, we used a time series analysis approach, combining elements of autoregressive and exponential smoothing models, with a nonlinear component, to gain a deeper understanding of how users' earnings/losses evolve over time. Our research may have broader implications for analyzing the dynamics of cryptocurrency transactions in decentralized systems, with possibilities for adapting the approach to study other multi-level platforms, such as Ponzi schemes, or even applying the methodology to traditional financial markets. Our data and analysis are available for public scrutiny, offering a transparent empirical research approach that can be built upon by the community. Our research paves the way for a more comprehensive study of Forsage and similar multi-level platforms, as well as contributing to the ongoing discussion about the future of cryptocurrency. The integrated properties of three promising globular cluster candidates, located in the outer regions of the Milky Way, have been examined in detail. Candidates G0210+0007, G0718+3311, and G0738+0001 were analyzed using high-resolution spectroscopy and imaging from the VLT/UVES, VLT/FLAMES, and Spitzer/IRAC, revealing age ranges of approximately 13.6-14.8 billion years for two clusters and 11.6-13.6 billion years for the third. These age ranges were determined through a combination of spectral and color analysis. Due to their distant location near the Galactic radius, these candidates offer valuable insights into the early development stages of the Milky Way. Additionally, a comparison with model predictions suggests that the cluster population in this region is lacking, implying an irregularity in mass distribution within this radial area. These findings contribute to a growing body of observations suggesting that globular clusters in the outer Galactic regions have an anomalous blue horizontal branch feature. More data are necessary to confirm the existence of these three candidates as confirmed globular clusters. If validated, they would increase the known number of globular clusters in the Milky Way by over 20%. These discoveries also highlight the importance of completing surveys for globular clusters in the Milky Way, as only about half of the possible clusters have been found so far. More extensive surveys from missions like Euclid and NGTS will provide a comprehensive understanding of the galaxy's cluster population and help solve the mystery of the galaxy's early development. This research addresses the challenge of predicting the transverse momentum distribution of particles in processes like $H \to b \bar b$, given that the masses of the individual quarks contribute significantly to the process's overall impact. A new observable has been developed to assess the impact of quark masses in a more comprehensive way, incorporating various orders of perturbative quantum chromodynamics. In addition, the study incorporates the effects of the strong interaction's renormalization group to ensure the accuracy of its predictions across a wide range of transverse momenta. The research demonstrates that quark-mass effects lead to a shift in the distribution's position and an increase in its normalized shape, and it provides a framework for estimating these effects in other processes in the future. The methodology will be applied to create more realistic simulated data that closely mimic the actual outcomes of processes like Higgs-boson production in particle collisions. The sensitivity of the steady-state quantum yield, once considered rare, now appears normal for reactions in complex environments and living organisms. This notion stems from the generalization of the Kasha rule to account for energy dissipation processes. However, the implication of this insight for photochemistry in complex systems and biological light sensors remains unclear. Using a stochastic model that describes the behavior of chromophores in solution and proteins, this study reveals how the average response to light intensity depends on the standard deviation of the distribution of decay rates available for relaxation. Specifically, it is shown that to enhance the sensitivity of the quantum yield to light intensity, there should be a limited range of decay rates available for relaxation and that this requirement is met in biological light sensors. Additionally, the relationship between the quantum yield and decay rates is analyzed to demonstrate that low-density regimes can exhibit over-sensitive behavior, giving advice on conducting related simulations. Finally, the differences between homogeneous and heterogeneous systems are explored to show that homogeneous systems can display sensitive behavior at higher densities, while heterogeneous systems can exhibit the same phenomenon at much lower density levels. Overall, this study suggests that the evolution of complex light sensors was driven by the need for systems that could respond differently to varying light intensities. This requirement could be met not just through changes in decay rates but also through changes in the standard deviation of these rates, influencing how organisms were selected and, in turn, influenced the direction of further evolution. In this sense, the unique properties of condensed-phase and biological systems make them ideal for the study of co-evolving light sensors and their chromophore components. Updatable simulations provide a powerful tool for this analysis, allowing for exploration of various scenarios, recovery of system parameters, and prediction of responses to changing environmental conditions. As such, this approach can be a model for the study of other co-evolving systems in science and philosophy.

To tackle dynamic business processes, models are needed that effectively predict future outcomes even when the process is partially complete. Yet, existing evaluation methods for these predictions typically focus on entire processes, neglecting the varying performance of models during different process stages. Our research introduces an innovative approach to evaluating predictions on business processes, allowing for the assessment of model performance at each process stage. We also present a method to identify stages with consistent prediction performance, enabling the application of a single model across those stages. Through experimentation, we demonstrate that our approach identifies stage-dependent prediction performance and facilitates model stage analysis. Furthermore, we reveal that predictions tend to perform well in early stages and may degrade in later stages due to evolving input data. Our approach and findings provide valuable insights for enhancing process outcomes and informing model maintenance decisions. These concepts are illustrated through an example simulation of inventory management and a real-world sales forecasting scenario. Our approach is adaptable to any data scenario and includes a modular design, making it easy to incorporate into existing algorithms via our publicly available implementation.
