This study introduces a novel approach to identifying names in low-resource languages, significantly enhancing the current standard of transfer learning for name tagging. Initially, our proposed method demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques in speech recognition and machine learning, respectively. Furthermore, our approach achieves substantial improvements in name tagging for low-resource languages, delivering a 6.48% enhancement in F-score on average according to the CONLL shared task annotations. Furthermore, our approach succeeds in incorporating a part-of-speech tagger, thereby expanding its application beyond name tagging. Our method comprises two primary modules. Firstly, a multi-task convolutional neural network is used for name representation and is trained with limited labeled data and abundant unsupervised text data. Secondly, a sequence-to-sequence module is employed for name tagging, supported by a trained character-level encoder. Our method showcases its effectiveness through name tagging experiments on three African languages, namely Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. All code and data used in this research are available online at https://github.com/odeyali/name-wiki.

Our study tracks the evolution of particle ratios in various collisions at LHC energies, specifically examining ratios of pions, protons, and phi mesons (identified via their $K^+K^-$ decay channel) as a function of transverse momentum ($p_T$) and centrality. We analyze data from 7 TeV-7 TeV and 5.02 TeV-2.76 TeV collisions, as well as 2.76 TeV-2.76 TeV collisions at LHC energies. Across all measured particle ratios, we observe a clear trend: as collision systems scale from the smallest to the largest, particle ratios at a given $p_T$ incrementally shift towards baseline values seen in elementary $pp$ collisions, with the magnitude of this shift correlated with the size of the collision system. This phenomenon suggests initial-state effects diminish with increasing collision volume. Additionally, our data reveal that centrality is not the sole driver of this behavior, as the transition from $pp$ to nucleus-nucleus collisions introduces additional variables that influence observed patterns. To further analyze $p_T$ distributions in various collisions, we've implemented detailed comparisons, including assessments of collective behavior and initial state conditions via event-shape selections. Lastly, our research highlights enhancements to particle ratio analyses, facilitated by enhanced precision in particle identification, as well as new detection capabilities for strange mesons (specifically $\phi$, $\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, $\Xi$) that will become relevant with future LHC data. Ultimately, our study sets the stage for in-depth investigations of quark matter properties within the LHC's kinetic range. The growing interest in building automated dialogue systems is driving the development of neural models for state tracking, which follow the overall structure of these interactions. However, creating and labeling the necessary data for these models is expensive, especially considering the extensive interaction history required for effective dialogue understanding. The presence of inaccurate labels in datasets can significantly impede the development of reliable models. The problem of learning from interactions that contain noisy labels poses a significant challenge for state tracking models, given the complexity of accurately identifying and correcting these errors. The objective of this work is to establish a method for developing a strong, robust dialogue state tracking model capable of processing interaction data containing noisy labels. The proposed approach involves using a technique called multi-task learning to build two models simultaneously. The first model is trained to excel in modeling accurate state representations, based on high-quality datasets, whereas the second model is trained to mimic the behavior of a state tracking model trained with noisy data. The combination of these two models yields a robust representation of state understandings, unmarred by the influence of inaccurate labels. The results of our experiments on the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge datasets demonstrate a notable improvement in performance, with an average error reduction of 4.3%. Similar to other complex systems, the onset and development of urban riots are highly unpredictable. There are multiple factors that contribute to this unpredictability. One of the key reasons is the urban landscape itself, which has a intricate network-based structure that affects the movement of individuals and the spread of information. This study introduces a mathematical approach to examine the dynamics of riots by modeling the interactions between citizens and a network representing the city's infrastructure. The model incorporates the concept of multiple "opinion" groups to account for differences in behavior among various demographic groups within the same community. Our findings reveal that the non-linear interaction between these groups, coupled with their movement within the city's infrastructure, can produce unstable equilibrium states, leading to the sudden emergence of widespread civil unrest. This model is applied to analyze the effectiveness of counter-measures such as identifying and isolating key demographic groups, which can significantly reduce the likelihood of the riots spiraling out of control. Our research offers a theoretical framework for analyzing the dynamics of urban riots and provides a foundation for future empirical investigations of this phenomenon. It is now possible to test this model using real-world data from cities that have experienced significant civil unrest. This model consists of multiple elements, including a power-law distribution that represents the varying sizes of demographic groups within the city's network structure, which is characterized by the co-existence of highly connected hubs and more isolated nodes. This unique architecture further amplifies the system's instability, making it prone to rapid changes and the sudden spread of unrest. This research has far-reaching implications, given the prevalence of civil unrest in many countries and the ongoing global trends of urbanization, demographic changes, and the spread of contagious ideas. It is now more important than ever to develop a deeper understanding of these complex urban dynamics to prevent and effectively manage the ongoing waves of global protests. This research has been publicly shared to solicit feedback from experts in the fields of sociology, economics, and physics. It is now possible to simulate the model using a mobile app, which is available for download on mobile devices and can be viewed at https://civilunrest.com. This app allows users to adjust key parameters, group sizes, and connection strengths within the city's network, as well as monitor the resulting dynamics in real-time. It is hoped that this research, including the mobile app, will provide a valuable platform for exploring the intricate dynamics of urban riots and informing strategies for preventing and managing these events. Because Br$\gamma$ luminosity is directly related to star formation rate, it was added to see if it would be used as such, which was confirmed. As a result, star formation rate estimates were influenced by Br$\gamma$ luminosity. Specifically, we found that using Br$\gamma$ luminosity instead of mass proxies reduces the scatter in star formation rate estimates by about a factor of two, and also improves the agreement between inferred and actual star formation rates, especially in the most massive galaxies. To use these findings effectively in future analyses, we also include instructions for adding Br$\gamma$ luminosity to mass proxy parameters in the Prospector framework. As an added benefit, using Br$\gamma$ luminosity helped improve the estimates of mass proxies themselves, reducing their scatter by about 30 percent. Ultimately, including Br$\gamma$ luminosity as an observable helps assess the accuracy of star formation rate estimates, and can be a valuable tool for inferring other galaxy properties as well. The FASERν experiment at CERN aims to investigate neutrino characteristics using neutrino beams from the decay of heavy flavor particles produced by the LHC. Specifically, it seeks to analyze 60 kton-year data sets from LHC runs at 14 TeV and 7 TeV, further divided into six energy intervals of O(1) GeV. These intervals allow for the study of neutrino interaction unitarity at a single neutrino energy level. Combining FASERν data with existing CKM unitarity constraints, we find the smallest deviation from total neutrino unitarity, ranging from 0.3 to 1.4 standard deviations, depending on the number of additional neutrino states and their masses. The contribution of FASERν to leptonic non-unitarity constraints is more significant than existing CKM unitarity constraints at O(10%) for all neutrino flavors except tau, where it is around O(5%). If no significant deviation from total unitarity is found, FASERν can tighten the constraint on non-unitarity by a factor of up to 9 in the 3-body decay channel, or by a factor of up to 27 in mass scales extending to O(1) eV, depending on the number of additional neutrino states and their masses. The FASERν results can also be applied to investigations of dark matter non-unitarity and its interactions with neutrinos in the 2-body decay channel. Ultimately, the unique capabilities of FASERν make it the most sensitive experiment for constraining neutrino non-unitarity in this context. The implications of these capabilities are explored in the context of several specific models, including the "dark" QCD and the "flavor anomaly" models, where FASERν can provide answers to outstanding questions and thereby demonstrate the effectiveness of its approach. The sensitivity of FASERν is further compared to that of next-generation neutrino experiments, such as T2HDO and GBAR, which, while more specialized, have different unitarity sensitivity profiles. In particular, FASERν can offer the tightest constraints in the energy range around O(40) GeV. In summary, FASERν has the capability to provide the most stringent limits on neutrino non-unitarity in its operating energy range, and its unique unitarity sensitivity profile makes it the most sensitive experiment for constraining neutrino non-unitarity in this context. Brzozowski's operator, which enables the derivation of a regular expression from a language defined by another regular expression, has been a fundamental concept in the study of regular expressions. Building upon earlier research, this paper expands Brzozowski's operator to support additional operations, including set difference and stars. Furthermore, it demonstrates that Brzozowski's operator can be the sole basis for a complete decision procedure to determine if one regular expression is contained within another. This procedure's effectiveness is established through a sequence of theoretical proofs. Additionally, this study introduces a novel algorithm to compute Brzozowski's operator for finite automata, which underpins the ability to perform complex operations with regular expressions. A universally available software has been created as a part of this research, enabling the efficient calculation of Brzozowski's operator for finite automata and the generation of regular expressions from specifications defined by automata. This software's capabilities are showcased through concrete examples. Moreover, this study's findings have significant implications for the development of software utilities that can perform tasks such as checking whether one regular expression is contained within another, or verifying if the union or intersection of two regular expressions equals a given regular expression. This research's contributions also include the introduction of a new Brzozowski's operator-based decision procedure and the development of an automated tool that can perform multiple tasks, including checking containment, intersection, and difference of regular expressions, as well as the conversion of finite automata to regular expressions. This research's results can help advance the state-of-the-art in computer science by making regular expressions a more versatile and adaptable specification language for programming languages. This research's findings can further contribute to the advancement of teaching methods and curriculum development in theoretical computer science courses. This research's work can also be extended to more complex formal languages, such as context-free languages, generating algorithms that can be employed in computer science applications, and facilitating the understanding of computer science concepts through visual demonstrations. This research's work can also be utilized in developing software utilities that can be part of programming languages, such as editors with built-in validation, and providing educational software for teaching formal language theory. This research's work can also be expanded to explore new properties and operators for regular expressions, such as Brzozowski's operator for star-free regular expressions, and developing new algorithms for finite automata. This research's work can also be used to study the computational complexity of Brzozowski's operator and decision procedures for regular expressions, and to investigate new decision procedures for containment and equivalence of regular expressions

Recent deep learning-based visual-inertial odometry (VIO) models have achieved impressive results with complex sequences, yet the underlying algorithms for many of these models remain poorly understood, especially when it comes to their placement within the VIO framework. This research aims to illuminate the structure of deep learning-based VIO models and clarify their connection to traditional approaches. We begin by providing an overview of the VIO pipeline and categorizing state-of-the-art VIO models based on their similarity to standard computer vision algorithms. We then delve into a comprehensive analysis of deep learning-based VIO models, focusing on their use of inertial and visual data. This involves detailing the structure of learning-based VIO models and assessing their adherence to fundamental inertial and visual processing principles. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings and presenting possible directions for future research in this area. This informative survey serves as a foundational resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to navigate the complex landscape of deep learning-based VIO models and the VIO framework as a whole. Three-dimensional Weyl semimetals possess unique physics resulting from their complex band structure, which includes high-order Weyl points, threefold degeneracies, and nodal lines. These features are linked to the square-root topology of Weyl semimetals. Research on iridate perovskites has revealed that they share the high-order Weyl point characteristics, but not the high-order Weyl point itself. These materials exhibit large anomalous Hall and Chern numbers generated by the closure of Weyl points and the creation of threefold degeneracies. Iridate perovskites belong to the group of materials that utilize the König seminar topological model. This research provides the theoretical framework for understanding the electronic and transport properties of these materials, which includes linearized and fully relativistic DFT calculations, and the construction of a Weyl semimetal Hamiltonian to simulate the electronic structure near the Fermi surface that surrounds the Weyl points. These efforts have yielded several key findings: (a) the generation of magnetic charges and charge currents in Weyl semimetals; (b) the formulation of a topological invariants diagram that illustrates the relationship between Weyl points and threefold degeneracies in materials with strong spin-orbit coupling; (c) the creation of a band-inversion diagram that illustrates the connection between Weyl points, threefold degeneracies, and nodal lines in materials with weak spin-orbit coupling. This research has also provided a microscopic explanation for the large anomalous Hall and Chern numbers observed in iridate perovskites. Lastly, this work has proposed that square-root topology be recognized as a fundamental concept that underlies the complex electronic structure of Weyl semimetals. This new framework is expected to guide further research into the unique physics of Weyl semimetals. Experimental verification of the predicted large anomalous Hall and Chern numbers in iridate perovskites is also recommended. Finally, this work is expected to pave the way for exploring other materials that exhibit high-order Weyl points characteristics but not the high-order Weyl point itself, such as honeycomb iridates and Ta/Ni doped half-heusler compounds, in the context of the König seminar topological model. This research has significant implications for our understanding of the electronic and transport properties of these complex materials. This study explores various finite element methods for solving data completion problems, particularly those involving the Laplace equation, on non-convex domains with discontinuous coefficient. Our research focuses on examining the influence of edge finite elements and their placement on the numerical solution. Edge elements are inherently suited to model interfaces between distinct domain regions. However, the performance of these finite element methods can be suboptimal if interfaces are not accurately represented. Our findings reveal that using edge elements alongside standard continuous elements within a complete Lagrange multipliers method yields optimal convergence rates. In contrast, utilizing nonconforming edge elements in conjunction with continuous elements leads to non-optimal convergence. On the other hand, edge elements alone are shown to achieve optimal convergence when coupled with a robust algebraic solver. Our research also highlights the advantage of employing edge elements exclusively over mixed finite elements. Notably, edge elements provide a more efficient and straightforward means of solving data completion problems, especially for large systems of equations. A priori error estimates are established through mesh independence and discrete compactness methods. Our numerical experiments are consistent with the theoretical findings and demonstrate the optimal convergence of solutions when edge elements are used alone. Additionally, the efficiency of edge elements is further demonstrated by a large-scale computation. The efficient performance of edge elements originates from their ability to accurately capture the optimal convergence of the algebraic solver. The results of this study can be applied to a broader class of equilibrium models that involve the Laplace equation, such as fluid pressure, membrane, and elasticity problems. The research is in line with the guidelines outlined in [3] and adds a crucial component to the existing error estimates. The study provides a more comprehensive understanding of the role of edge finite elements in solving data completion problems and highlights the suboptimal performance of certain methods. The research is relevant to a wide range of applications and could benefit the development of robust, adaptable numerical methods. The implementation of the edge element method is accompanied by a publicly accessible code. The research is part of the author's dissertation and was presented at the 2019 ICIAM Congress in Valencia, Spain. The study has a direct connection to but is distinct from the author's related research in [4] and [5]. The paper has undergone significant revisions based on the feedback received at the 2020 MathML meeting in Boston, Massachusetts. This paper delves into the characterization of the parafermion type vertex operator algebra associated with the simple affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$. We outline the specific generators and quasi-polynomial characters associated with this algebra, as well as the construction of intertwining operators that map $osp(1|2n)$ modules to $so(2n+1)$ modules. Building upon this, we establish the extension of these algebras to lattices and fermion algebras, and examine their associated vertex operator algebras and intertwining operators. Finally, we derive an equivalence relating the characters of $osp(1|2n)$ highest weight modules to the characters of certain $so(2n+1)$ highest weight modules, giving an extension valid across all central charges. This latter result is then utilized to formulate an invitation to study the spectral distribution of $osp(1|2n)$ characters through the application of quantum field theory symmetry. Lastly, we outline methods to adapt this analysis to Lie superalgebras affiliated with $osp(1|2m)$, $osp(1|2n)$, or $osp(1|2m,2n)$.

This study introduces an innovative paradigm in knowledge transfer, where a student model learns from a more experienced teacher model that is deliberately flawed. The goal is to improve the student by identifying and rectifying the errors embedded in the teacher, whose performance is now amplified as a result of this saliency-based approach. Unlike traditional methods that assume the teacher always produces accurate and diverse knowledge, this approach allows for multiple representations of the same concept. A highly relevant data example can now be considered an instance of the same concept, enabling distance-based amalgamation. Our method incorporates a pair of tasks: a discrimination task that pinpoints defects in the teacher and a correction task that refines the flawed knowledge. A complementary attention mechanism is proposed to address the increased risk of overfitting and alleviate the teacher's load. Experimental findings show that our approach not only accurately pinpoints defects in the teacher but also effectively amalgamates knowledge from diverse sources, outperforming current state-of-the-art knowledge distillation methods when data is limited. Although the brain's spatial coding relies on multiple areas with distinct functions, it's unclear how external cues influence the performance of individual cell types. We used a combination of psychophysical experimentation and neural recording in rats to gain insight into the operating principles of grid cells under various environmental conditions. Our results reveal how external cues affect the size of grid cells' spatial coverage based on visual, tactile, and navigational factors. When multiple cues are available, they compete for control of grid cells' activity patterns, and this competition can result in the dominance of conflicting sensory inputs. Our findings also suggest that grid cells' response to local navigation is rooted in distinct directional preferences rather than a global representation of spatial orientation. Furthermore, our data indicate that the format in which angular path information is processed varies significantly when only considering short-distance navigation. Ultimately, our research shows that the spatial coverage of grid cells is shaped by the interplay between external cues, their salience, and the animal's internal state and movement history. This perspective on grid cells challenges the long-held view of these cells as maintainers of a constant, self-updated mental map of spatial position and orientation. Instead, we propose a new framework in which grid cells are seen as sensors that monitor changes to spatial coverage in real-time, and where the meaning of this coverage is determined by the competition among external cues and the animal's internal movement dynamics. This concept is particularly relevant to predictive coding theories of neural function. By incorporating grid cells with similar functions to those reported here, we can refine existing models of predictive coding and test the implications for our understanding of neural circuits involved in spatial coding. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of considering multiple levels of perception and how they interact to understand the complex functioning of brain areas with multiple, overlapping functions. It demonstrates that, even in areas with seemingly well-isolated functions, as much as 90% of cellular activity can be influenced by external cues, and that, even in areas with well-defined functional roles, as much as 70% of cellular activity can be confounded by conflicting sensory inputs. In this context, we propose a new framework for analyzing neural data, one that prioritizes the identification of intrinsic and extrinsic factors that compete for control of neural circuits' activity patterns. This approach is particularly relevant to our current understanding of grid cells, and it could also provide valuable new insights into other areas of neural circuitry. We examined the interface states at the channel surface of p-type silicon MOSFETs, depending on whether the silicon was etched or treated with buffer oxide etching.  By comparing the results, we found a higher carrier concentration near the surface when etched silicon is used, which is attributed to the reduction of surface tail states.  A higher carrier concentration was measured at 1.38 x 10^18 per cm^3, which is a result of etched silicon having a more conductive path than usual.  This effect on carrier concentration was found to be consistent across different etching solutions.  In contrast, oxide etching, which removes a greater thickness of silicon, results in a higher doping concentration but also causes oxide trapped charges that negatively affect the MOSFET's threshold voltage.  This analysis indicates that etched silicon can increase carrier concentration and reduce threshold voltage without compromising the MOSFET's performance.  This simple and cost-effective method offers a straightforward way to enhance the performance of MOSFETs.  As a result, etched silicon is an attractive alternative to expensive and complex processes such as dopant segregation or source/drain engineering.  To validate these findings, we conducted SPICE simulations using a real-device model, which showed a significant improvement in current drive capability and intrinsic gain after treating the silicon in this way.  Consequently, etched silicon has significant potential for further improving the performance of advanced MOSFETs. The evolution of a planet's atmosphere may be shaped by a cycle between its internal and external components, potentially leading to diverse outcomes, including atmospheric loss, habitable conditions, or extreme environments. This process's timescale could be comparable to a planet's age, influencing whether significant changes occur during its early stages or later stages of development. Interior-atmospheric interactions are governed by processes like convection, corotation radiation, or stellar gravitational forces, which have different timescales and can result in interior cycling rates varying greatly across various planets. The rate of exterior-atmospheric interactions is largely determined by solar wind dynamics, but may be affected by factors like the presence of a stellar magnetosphere or a planetary magnetosphere's effectiveness. As a result, planets with similar interior characteristics but differing exterior environments may exhibit distinct atmospheric trajectories, potentially leading to diverse outcomes, including habitable conditions, extreme environments, or atmospheric loss, and affecting whether changes occur during their early stages or later stages of development. These adjustments involve setting a particular mass ratio in the doublet system to approximately 1, establishing a direct connection between the value of this ratio and the magnitude of the tau dipole moment. Furthermore, our findings indicate that large CP-violating effects can arise solely as a result of one or more of the heavy Higgs bosons possessing masses in the range of several hundred GeV to just below the W and Z boson masses. This scenario also predicts that the W and Z boson masses will exhibit a slight deviation from their Standard Model values, with an absolute difference of less than 10^-3. This deviation can be distinguished from the Standard Model through precision experiments with a margin of error of less than 3 sigma. This paper delves into the error-correcting capabilities of rank-metric codes, either alone or in combination with polar codes, especially focusing on decoding under the rank metric. We initially examine decoding strategies for single codes with high error correction capabilities, either using the sliding window decoder or the polar code decoder, depending on the code rate. Our findings show that for code rates below 1/2, unipolar mint codes exhibit high error correction capabilities, up to half of the code length, and can correct errors in up to n/2 - 1 symmetric channels. In contrast, for code rates above 1/2, we propose a method to generate rank-metric codes from polar codes, providing the same benefits of efficient decoding under the rank metric. Finally, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining rank-metric codes with polar codes, offering superior error correction capabilities, particularly for code rates above 1/2, and offers suggestions for optimizing code lengths and error correction capacities in various symmetric channels. Our proposals contribute relevant concepts to the design of codes under the rank metric. Additionally, our code constructions facilitate further research into the study of error correction capacities in multi-letter channels and the generalization of rank-metric polar codes to other metric spaces. Our code constructions and findings are publicly available at https://github.com/ujjwal1086/PMCS-submission.

This adaptation successfully demonstrated its effectiveness, surpassing the state-of-the-art in low-rank factorization techniques and even outperforming supervised deep learning approaches with a significantly reduced number of required training notes. This research introduces an original approach to investigating the behavior of rotating stars, which involves treating fluid particles with defined properties such as mass and angular momentum in a differential form that reflects their global impact. In this framework, the fluid's potential energy is re-expressed and a simplified equation derived, resulting in a form similar to the Euler-Poisson equation, which can be solved numerically to model rotating stars. To test this method, we created a benchmark scenario based on a slowly rotating star model similar to CPSC, which resulted in minimal deviations in our results when compared to traditional methods, with minor adjustments required to match potential energy and angular momentum levels. However, our approach demonstrates its ability to handle more rapidly rotating stars, producing multiple co-rotating branches within a given scenario. Ultimately, this new framework provides an opportunity to study highly rotating stars with extreme specific angular momentum, potentially resembling stars born in certain binary mergers. This could help explain the origins of intermediate mass black hole candidates weighing in at roughly fifty solar masses. In this context, our approach enables us to identify new potential targets, such as PS1-10cz and V3795 Sgr, which may result from the merger of intermediate mass black holes and neutron stars, producing stars with massive angular momentum. These stars are then shed into space over millions of years, holding clues to their cosmic events. This approach also allows us to recognize distinct landmarks within rotation diagrams of stars, making it a powerful tool for predicting the outcomes of future gravitational wave observations. This methodology can be adapted for use in studies of rotating stellar clusters, leading to novel perspectives on the behavior of these types of stars. We've developed a novel method for learning machine learning models that can handle partial or selective labeling. This is particularly useful when labeling is expensive or time-consuming, as it significantly reduces the necessary computational resources. Moreover, we've found that utilizing selective labeling leads to improved performance in regression tasks and comparable performance in classification tasks, all while significantly cutting labeling costs in half. Additionally, we've explored various strategies for selecting key instances for labeling and have found that a simple, low-cost method produces the best outcomes. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdwang/Selective-Labeling. Our research indicates that selective labeling can cut labeling costs in half without a decline in model performance, making it a viable technique for reducing the expense of acquiring labeled data.

Previous studies in machine learning have shown that contextual information plays a crucial role in modeling real-language contexts, and this research seeks to explore the implications of contextual modeling on machine learning models' ability to identify false information. Our findings indicate that contextual models are more likely than non-contextual models to distinguish true from false information, and this superiority can be attributed to the transfer of this ability to unsupervised situations. In scenarios where little knowledge about the false information is available and only a limited number of false articles can be learned from context, our research reveals that contextual models outperform non-contextual models. In environments with extensive training datasets and a diverse range of false information at hand, our studies suggest that contextual models perform similarly to non-contextual models. In contrast, unsupervised approaches yielded mixed results and consistently outperformed the corresponding context-based models in all evaluation tasks. This research calculates two-loop corrections to the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators in N=4 SYM theory using a combination of integrand method and string theory in AdS$_5$ x S$^5$. Specifically, we determine the two-loop anomalous dimensions of the operators O_{4;2}(z,\bar z) and O_{4;4}(z,\bar z)$ for both BPS and non-BPS cases. Our string theory calculations are performed with $\alpha'^2 N c=1$, and we compare our results to available two-loop holographic anomalous dimension data in the SYM four-point function, finding a match up to an overall O(N^2) coefficient. We also address the issue of boundary contribution divergence in the AdS bulk gauge theory, proposing a regularisation technique that allows us to obtain finite two-loop anomalous dimensions from the string theory side. We analyze our BPS dimension results in the context of existing mathematical derivations, and present an explicit proof of the relevant double-sine formula using the string theory approach. We further explore the general formula for an arbitrary impact factor k, and demonstrate its applicability to previously unstudied twist-three operators in the SYM four-point function. Finally, we discuss potential applications of our two-loop anomalous dimension results to studies of BPS observable charges in N=4 SYM theory.

As GPUs become an essential component in high-performance computing systems, understanding GPU memory virtualization has become crucial. The lack of a publically available GPU memory allocator that can be safely virtualized has been identified as a significant issue. To address this, we introduced SOAr, a stateful GPU memory allocator, which provides reliable memory management and enhances performance. However, SOAr's efficiency is hindered by its high overhead and slow memory reclamation, especially when dealing with large-scale applications. To mitigate this limitation, we have evolved SOAr into DynaSOAr, which utilizes dynamic state management to optimize memory allocation and reclamation. In DynaSOAr, we leverage asynchronous transactions to coordinate thread access to memory segments, thereby minimizing synchronization delays. Furthermore, we implemented a segment management system that dynamically responds to memory evictions, reclaims memory segments, and merges overlapping segments to prevent unnecessary memory waste. In conjunction with asynchronous memory reclamation, DynaSOAr's performance is significantly improved, allowing it to achieve speed-ups of up to 8.2x and 3.3x in memory allocation and reclamation, respectively, when compared to the baseline allocator. In addition, DynaSOAr has been integrated with PGAS languages such as Gyra and Francium, enabling seamless use of GPU memory virtualization. This paper investigates the boundedness properties of operators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces, particularly focusing on the operators that are continuously embedded or divergent. Recently, Q. Jiang and J. Li characterized the continuous embedding operators on mixed Morrey spaces. Building on their work, this paper explores the applications of those results to operators on the mixed Morrey spaces. Specifically, it examines the boundedness of sublinear operators and a class of fractional integral operators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Moreover, this paper obtains the boundedness criteria for the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund operators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces, assuming the smoothness condition of the kernels. Finally, this paper provides the boundedness proof for the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on the GMMSp_{p,q}, and establishes the quasi-boundedness of the Calderón-Zygmund operators on the generalized mixed Morrey spaces, when p = 1. All the obtained results are advancements over the existing standards and can be seen as extensions to the original works by T. X. Huang and Y. Q. Zhang on Morrey spaces and by Q. Jiang and J. Li on mixed Morrey spaces. Moreover, this paper includes an auxiliary inequality that may be useful in exploring the boundedness of other operators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Lastly, this paper is dedicated to Professor Y. Zhang as a token of appreciation for his contributions to the field of operator theory.

Our combined scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy study examines the impact of spin-orbit coupling on locally tailored surface states at a copper surface, modified by adatoms or dimers of iron and cobalt. When the spin-orbit coupling is weak, as with copper, we find that dimers enhance the symmetry of states around vortices, while adatoms create millipede states due to their proximity. Introducing stronger spin-orbit coupling with selenium, however, alters the millipede state at selenium adatoms but not at copper adatoms within the investigated energy range. Interestingly, we observe that selenium dimers can form both millipede and local state at vortices at certain positions on the spectrum. A theoretical model shows that dimers can exhibit both millipede and local states based on their relative energies of d-orbitals, and that the sensitivity to spin-orbit coupling varies with chemical ingredients and their spatial separation. Consequently, dimers represent a more complex and adjustable tool for manipulating surface states compared to adatoms. Our findings also highlight the potential for experimental design of Yashonova-Siamese-rod states by controlling the chemical composition of dimers. Ultimately, this capability may enable the realization of topological insulator states in thin films mediated by spin-orbit coupling.

This study confirms the existence of totally enclosed, finite-width minimal disks in three-dimensional space, thereby exploring their connection to the spectral properties of specific submanifolds. Additionally, we establish the non-radial nature of these minimal disks. Building upon previous findings, we demonstrate that in two-dimensional Euclidean space, there are non-round, complete and bounded minimal disks. This result is linked to the presence of interior eigenvalues less than one for certain subdomains within the original disk. A similar relationship between non-round, finite-width minimal disks in three-dimensional space and the presence of interior eigenvalues equal to one for certain subdomains within the original sphere is also established. This research is an expansion of earlier work by the first author, where the existence of finite-width, enclosed minimal disks in two and four-dimensional space was proven. The methods employed here are distinct and provide new insights. The proof of non-radiality is achieved through a technique involving the symmetrization of functions, allowing for greater flexibility in higher-dimensional spaces. The non-round nature of the minimal disks is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of the spectral mean formula, followed by an examination of the eigenvalues and shapes of the corresponding flat subdomains within the original manifold. This research also establishes an interesting connection between the non-round nature of these minimal disks and the presence of particular interior eigenvalues for the associated Schr\"{o}dinger operator. Lastly, this research is presented in a way that is accessible to mathematicians across various disciplines. It begins with an introduction to the problem at hand, followed by an overview of previously established results in this area. The basic properties of minimal surfaces are then reviewed, along with a detailed explanation of the associated linear Schr\"{o}dinger operator and its eigenvalues. The paper is structured to be understandable to those familiar with the basics of both geometric and analytical geometry. It also provides new insights for experts in these fields. A new approach is proposed to analyze cloud shapes using topological methods and image processing techniques. This method focuses on identifying key characteristics in satellite images, particularly with regards to moluccus-type clouds, which have a distinctive core surrounded by thick layers of precipitation, often hidden from view. By applying topological and kinematic principles, this analysis reveals the core's presence and the surrounding precipitation's movement patterns. A mathematical model is then used to map the cloud's structure and predict its future shape. This method is highly relevant to the study of moluccus clouds, which can produce heavy rainfall that may last for several days and is crucial to understanding the regional water cycle. However, observing these clouds is challenging due to their location and the need for very high resolution satellite images. A notable example studied here is the cloud system that caused rainfall in the Kayan Mountains of Myanmar in 2014. By applying the proposed analysis methods to satellite images, the characteristics of these clouds can be better understood, and their shapes and movement patterns can be more accurately predicted. This research was conducted by a single author and utilizes data from the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission and the Multi-spectral Imaging Spectrometer. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this analysis approach in identifying cloud characteristics, structure, and movement, and it is hoped that this method will contribute to the advancement of cloud research and the development of more precise weather forecasting models. Four additional clouds were also analyzed using this method, and the results reveal a previously unseen type of cloud called the 'anemone cloud'. This cloud features a thick, stationary core surrounded by thinner layers of precipitation that resemble an anemone flower. The movement of these clouds is significant, with some extending over 300km in a week. It is anticipated that this method of analysis will provide new insights into cloud research and facilitate the development of more effective weather forecasting models. The source code for this research is available online. The method described here has the potential to analyze other types of clouds as well. The author suggests that cloud researchers and scientists collaborate to apply this method to a broader range of clouds and to share their findings. The author also proposes that this approach be made available as a cloud service to facilitate its use across the field of cloud research. The approach presented in this study is the basis for the development of a new weather forecasting model, and the author suggests that this model be tested and validated in conjunction with satellite and ground-based observations. A notable finding in astronomy, Kepler-452b, has been used to inspire research on a
specific type of exoplanet: mini-Neptunes with surfaces suitable for life. To identify
these "Earthlike" Neptunes, researchers have determined the parameters for a new
classification system based on data from the Kepler space telescope. Using this
framework, they have discovered two new candidates, both of which are located in the
habitable zones of their respective stars. Kepler-1229b and Kepler-1541b, the two
planets, have dimensions similar to that of the Earth and orbit their stars in regions
where liquid water could potentially exist on their surfaces. A mini-Neptune is
defined as having a mass between 5 to 20 times that of the Earth and a diameter
between 1.4 to 2.7 times the Earth's diameter. To validate these discoveries,
astronomers plan to conduct follow-up observations with the Spitzer and Kepler
space telescopes. If confirmed, these findings could mark the beginning of a new
era in the search for life beyond the Earth. A report detailing this research has
been accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal. This study is part of
the Kepler EarthView project, which aims to discover three to four Earthlike
mini-Neptunes within a specific type of star system. To achieve this goal, the
research team employed a strategy that involved targeting a particular type of star
system characterized by moderate temperatures and slow rotation rates. Using this
approach, the team has analyzed a total of 615 days of data from the Kepler space
telescope and identified a total of 11,600 candidate planets within a subset of
15,000 targets. To date, this research has led to the discovery of two accepted
planetary candidates and several upper limits for a various types of planets across
different sizes and orbital periods. To improve the accuracy of its findings, the
Kepler EarthView project employs a multi-step data analysis process that involves
both automated and manual reviews. To minimize false positives, the team uses a
range of algorithms that identify unusual patterns in the data. Once potential
planets are identified, the team conducts a detailed analysis of each candidate's
light curve, followed by a manual review of the data in search of signs of
planetary activity. To validate these findings, the researchers plan to conduct

We have conducted a comprehensive investigation into the behaviors of carbon and nitrogen when they occupy interstitial positions within anatase TiO2, using both experimental techniques and computer simulations. Our studies reveal significant variations in the properties of these atoms when placed inside the crystal structure, as opposed to when they substitute for atoms within the TiO2 lattice. Our findings indicate that both interstitial and lattice-location atoms of carbon and nitrogen possess an excess of electrons that are easily lost, which could enhance their ability to act as acceptors of electrons. Our research also identifies a direct correlation between the sizes of these atoms and their tendency to occupy a vacant space within the TiO2 structure, with larger atoms being more likely to do so. We have further determined that the energy released from these atoms as they occupy interstitial positions is so great that it surpasses any barriers that might exist to their entry into the TiO2 structure. Our studies using computer simulations also demonstrate that both interstitial and lattice-location atoms of carbon and nitrogen are capable of existing within TiO2 without causing any significant damage to the crystal structure. We have assigned a charge of one to all these atoms based on their electronic interactions with neighboring oxygen atoms, and we have established that they possess a high reactivity that could either benefit their utilization in catalytic applications or impede the stability of TiO2 when they accumulate in sufficient numbers. We have a special interest in the behaviors of these atoms when they are exposed to light, and we have used computer simulations to study their absorption of visible light. Our analysis of the results of these studies indicates that both interstitial and lattice-location atoms of carbon and nitrogen have the capacity to act as centers for the absorption of light, and we have identified several key factors that influence this ability, including their location within the TiO2 crystal structure, their atomic size, and the amount of charge they possess. We have also found that interstitial atoms are more likely than lattice-location atoms to exhibit a high level of light absorption, and that this phenomenon could either enhance or impede the performance of TiO2 in photodynamic therapy, depending on additional factors. We have a particular concern about the potential health effects of using TiO2 containing interstitial carbon or nitrogen atoms in respiratory applications, and we have expressed a need for further research in this area. We have expressed a hope that our studies will contribute to a better understanding of the behaviors of carbon and nitrogen within TiO2 and will ultimately lead to a development of strategies for controlling their location and properties within this crystal structure

The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on the Athena telescope will study the intra-cluster medium (ICM) by mapping the X-ray spectra of various fields within a cluster. Due to the ICM's turbulent nature, the X-IFU will encounter a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. The data analysis for such a powerful instrument requires a sophisticated framework that can handle the complexities of data processing, spectroscopic analysis, and astrophysical turbulence modeling. We present an overview of the X-IFU analysis framework called XIFU-AF, which incorporates existing software tools such as ADAS, TAOS, and FIbfS. The framework includes data processing via Field by Field Spectroscopy (FbfS) and further analysis of spatial and temporal turbulence scales through the development of time-series spectral maps. The current implementation of XIFU-AF uses Python with additional C++ elements for critical steps. The framework has been demonstrated with mock data generated by the Athena X-IFU simulation tool called AXIFU-SIM and is available on GitHub under a 3-clause BSD license. The code can be adapted for other X-ray instruments, such as those on the Euclid satellite, and is the basis for ongoing discussions within the scientific community. The future directions for the project involve collaborating with other analysis framework developers, accessing real data, and refining the techniques for turbulence parameter estimation. The code's simplicity and modular design allow for easy customization and integration with other astrophysics turbulence simulation frameworks. The approach presented in XIFU-AF represents a significant step forward in the development of robust data analysis methods for X-ray instruments and can contribute to the successful operation of the X-IFU on board the Athena telescope. The project's code and documentation are available at https://github.com/ruippeca/XIFU-AF and will be continuously updated on GitHub. The discussion on the project's forum at https://forum.atacam-telescope.org/c/x-ifu-af-atacama-france-3 remains open to the community. The project's code is licensed under a 3-clause BSD license. A face-scanning biometric system relies on accurate face detection to function effectively. Although the advancement of machine learning techniques has enhanced the performance of this system, several vulnerabilities still exist in its current implementation. A constrictive approach to developing this system is proposed, which involves reducing the necessary input from the entire face to a focused area - in this case, the eye region. This approach offers several advantages, including: 1) simpler and more robust eye-focused detection being capable of tolerating minor angular deviations, occlusions, and lighting discrepancies; 2) improved user experience resulting from eye-focused authentication systems that are easier to operate and tolerate slight eye movements; 3) secured against presentation attacks by employing dual-validation - a method that verifies both eye features and face structure to prevent fraud. Experimental results show that the eye-focused detection method can accommodate up to 45 degrees of eye movement and reduce authentication time by half. Moreover, this system has potential applications in various eye-focused biometric systems, offering a balanced approach to security and user convenience. Our investigation assesses how accurately the mass of particles can be determined by measuring the characteristics of qubits and qutrits when subjected to various forms of error. Specifically, we convolve different error channels with two precision-measuring techniques: qubit and qutrit state tomography, and the interferometric readout technique. Our findings indicate some error channels have a greater impact on the mass determination of qubits than qutrits, while reversing this dynamic in other error conditions. Furthermore, our research reveals that in some scenarios, measuring the properties of a system can provide more reliable mass determinations than interferometric readout. However, this advantage comes with increased requirements for classical processing and an increased number of measurements. Our study also shows that, for a particular error channel, the mass determination accuracy in qutrits can surpass that of qubits by a factor of approximately $2^{7.5}$. To experimentally verify these theoretical predictions, we propose using current trapped ion technology. Our study highlights the potential for exploring new phenomena related to phase space reconstruction in quantum systems. Ultimately, our research suggests that studying the mass properties of particles offers a unique approach to investigating fundamental quantum properties and their consequences. This approach may contribute to the development of quantum systems that can withstand decoherence and noise. In this context, our findings provide insights into the relative robustness of qubits and qutrits under various error conditions, which could influence the choice of system for specific applications. Nonetheless, our investigation reveals that neither qubit nor qutrit systems can guarantee consistently reliable mass determination in the presence of noise, which has significant implications for the development of quantum systems based on these particles. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the necessity for a broader discussion about the relationships between quantum systems, their applications, and the concepts of stability and robustness. This discussion will be crucial as we move forward with the development of quantum systems and their potential uses. The findings from our analysis are also relevant to any system that can exist in a multi-level system and is susceptible to various forms of decoherence, making it relevant to a wide range of systems beyond just qubits and qutrits. We explore the concept of polynomial diameter in finite groups, establishing connections with conjugacy class sizes and the presence of nilpotent subgroups. Our findings reveal that group classes with a polynomial diameter have a restricted layout, characterized by a minimal number of large conjugacy classes and a substantial number of nilpotent subgroups, with the exception of a sparse set of exceptional cases. Furthermore, we identify a clear distinction between our results and recent class size theory, as our polynomials of small degree can be any degree, not just linear or quadratic. Ultimately, we apply our findings to establish the polynomial diameter conjecture for a specific, though limited, class of groups – those with a high probability ratio. We analyzed how neighboring point information affects classification performance in 3D LiDAR scans and found that context has a limited impact due to distant range gates, thereby enabling the substitution of neighboring points with batch-wise sampled points for enhanced diversity. By leveraging this observation, we developed a novel deep learning model called ScatterNet that combines three key features to classify 3D point clouds from LiDAR data: 1) efficient sampling of range gates; 2) enhanced input feature diversity; and 3) learned global point cloud representations. In comparison to existing deep learning approaches, our method achieves superior classification accuracy across multiple datasets and metrics. Notably, it outperforms previous results in the ISPRASmall dataset by a 2.3% margin and surpasses the classification performance in the S3DC dataset by 1.3% in the single-branch setting. Moreover, our scatter-based sampling strategy and batch-wise sampling mechanism can be applied to other 3D point cloud segmentation models. By addressing limitations in previous works and showcasing compelling results, we anticipate that ScatterNet will serve as a benchmark for LiDAR-based 3D classification tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/zeze352/ScatterNet.

Further collaborative research between neutrino and ultra-high-energy cosmic ray experiments is highly recommended to uncover potential connections between these phenomena. The methods presented here can serve as a framework for conducting such analyses in the future.

Recent studies have used machine learning to analyze the behavior of automatic essay scoring systems. Despite some progress, there remains a significant need for more comprehensive research on the subject. Our work addresses this gap by examining the performance of complex machine learning models in evaluating complex tests. We specifically investigated whether advanced automatic essay scoring systems exhibit unstable or inconsistent behavior when minor changes are made to test questions. To study this, we developed a technique to systematically vary the content of test questions and analyze the response of automatic essay scoring systems. We applied this approach to data from a real-world high-stakes testing administration. Our results showed that even when scoring systems are otherwise accurate, they can produce unreliable results for certain test takers. We also found that these irregular performances are not unique to specific scoring systems or administrators, but rather a feature of the systems themselves. Moreover, we identified specific sources of instability in these scoring systems, including their tendency to overemphasize certain aspects of writing and underestimate others. Our research provides a framework for evaluating the reliability of automatic essay scoring systems and identifying instances of unstable performance. We recommend that future research be conducted with a broader range of test content and scoring systems to further understand the implications of these findings. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of both developing better automatic essay scoring systems and conducting rigorous evaluations of these systems in real-world settings. As a byproduct of our study, we developed several metrics for assessing the reliability of automatic essay scoring systems, which can also be applied to other machine learning models that evaluate written content. These metrics have the potential to contribute to a new area of research focused on the robustness of machine learning models in education. Additionally, our work includes an analysis of how these systems perform when evaluating different demographic groups, although our current findings indicate no significant differences in performance across these groups. Nevertheless, we believe that future research is necessary to fully understand how these systems perceive the varied writing skills present in educational assessments. In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive investigation of the complex behavior exhibited by automatic essay scoring systems and proposes a range of research focused on evaluating the robustness and reliability of these systems. This work is particularly relevant given the widespread adoption of these systems in high-stakes educational assessments and the inherent importance of ensuring the validity and reliability of such assessments. As a result of this study, we are committed to conducting further research with various machine learning models that evaluate written content, assessing their robustness and reliability, and contributing to the development of robust machine learning models for educational applications. Nucleus detection is a fundamental task in medical analysis, with accurate automatic detection being crucial for subsequent analysis and treatment planning. Existing methods, while effective, are often slow and difficult to expand to detect other structures. In response, we propose an innovative, resource-friendly approach called the W-shaped network, which incorporates dual encoding blocks and utilizes the network's intermediate features to detect multiple objects. By leveraging a nifty workaround for attribute sharing, the W-shaped network significantly enhances detection efficiency with minimal computational overhead. When applied to nucleus detection, it achieves exceptional performance on various datasets with a notable decrease in parameters and floating point operations, surpassing even state-of-the-art fast methods. Moreover, the W-shaped network proves adaptable, easily extrapolating to detect other structures such as cells and organs. With its versatility and efficient design, the W-shaped network is an exemplary solution for automatic object detection in medical analysis. To facilitate further research, we've made our code and model publicly available. Moreover, we've introduced the AutoNucleus challenge, along with a dataset specifically designed to test nucleus detection, along with comprehensive rules and evaluation criteria. This challenge aims to propel the development of highly efficient detection methods, addressing the growing need for fast and accurate medical analysis. The Hamiltonian path index of a graph H is the minimum number of hamiltonian paths needed to cover all vertices of H. We explore the relationship between hamiltonian paths and hamiltonian path index by examining specific graphs that have multiple hamiltonian paths, particularly focus is given on cubic graphs. A new formula for the hamiltonian path index of line graphs is derived, and it is demonstrated that this index can be 2 when the original graph is a line graph. Further, the index can be 3 for certain cubic graphs, and this is shown to be the minimum number of hamiltonian paths for these graphs as no hamiltonian cycles exist within them. An approach using the junction technique is introduced to determine the hamiltonian path index of these cubic graphs. An example of a cubic graph with 8 vertices where the hamiltonian path index is 2 is provided, and it is proposed that this may hold as the minimum number of hamiltonian paths for all such graphs. No proof is given for this proposal, but it is suggested that further research is required to validate or refute it. In an attempt to slow COVID-19's spread, many countries imposed restrictive anti-virus measures, yet these efforts haven't prevented the rise in COVID-19 cases across the globe. This steadfast increase in COVID-19 cases prompts us to reevaluate our understanding of the disease's progression, which might be misinterpreted due to insufficient data. We propose that COVID-19's growth surge results from cell death caused by a previous infection, which releases infected cells bursting with viral particles, thereby infecting nearby cells and continuing the cycle. This theory could be validated through magnetic resonance imaging by identifying the time-dependent change in water diffusion in lung tissue, providing insight into the underlying pathology. If this approach is feasible, it may allow us to assess the effectiveness of existing and potential treatments, such as anti-inflammatory medications, which could alter the disease's course by either slowing cell death or facilitating host immune system recovery. We also suggest modifying existing MRI technology to enhance virus visualization through magnetic resonance imaging techniques. We believe that adopting this approach will be beneficial in comprehending COVID-19's progression and identifying suitable treatment options.

In the context of automated program verification, logical pseudocodes serve as precise descriptions of algorithms in a formal language. These codes are often contrasted with traditional pseudocodes, which prioritize readability for humans. Research has focused on the properties of logical pseudocodes, leaving the differences between them and traditional pseudocodes unexplored. By analyzing the design of both types of pseudocodes, this paper reveals the distinct features that ensure the correctness and safety of logical pseudocodes, demonstrating the equivalency of logical and operational semantics in programming languages via the correctness theorem of programming by reflection. This conceptual framework can guide the development of programming languages and algorithms with built-in correctness proofs, effectively merging verification and implementation. By leveraging this approach, the performance benefits of optimal algorithms can be achieved while avoiding the limitations of suboptimal algorithms, which sacrifice efficiency for ease of implementation. Ultimately, this paper advocates for the use of logical pseudocodes as the standard means of algorithmic expression, enabling the automatic generation of algorithms that are both efficient and correct. As a concrete application, this approach has been employed to develop a method for finding the minimum length of a counterfactual formula in saturated propositional logic with negation, which can be used to create a procedure for this task. This procedure constitutes the first example of a feature-based algorithm in first-order logic. The concepts explored in this paper have broader implications, enabling the development of optimal algorithms that are both effective and efficient, capable of being applied to various domains, including the analysis of counterfactuals in saturated propositional logic with negation, the evaluation of extended endomorphisms in free groups, and the examination of action sequences in endomorphisms of free groups with a generating set containing inverses. As such, this approach opens up new possibilities for the automated creation of optimal algorithms for these and other domains. As a demonstration of this potential, a new algorithm has been created to solve a previously unaddressed problem related to action sequences in endomorphisms of free groups with a generating set containing inverses. This novel algorithm was independently crafted by hand and verified by the proof assistant Isabelle, demonstrating the feasibility of this approach. As a result of this research, the distinction between traditional and logical pseudocodes has become clearer, demonstrating the superiority of logical pseudocodes in terms of correctness and safety. As such, this paper argues that logical pseudocodes should become the standard means of algorithmic expression, enabling the automatic creation of efficient and effective algorithms. A one-pass algorithm is proposed for creating a small representation of data regarding the $k$-means clustering problem. Unlike previous methods, this algorithm does not require access to the optimal centers and can handle non-metric distances. It results in a cluster core that accurately reflects the optimal $k$-means cluster configuration, both in terms of point distribution and weights. The size of the core is proportional to $k$, $p$, and the logarithm of the dimensionality for Euclidean distance, and only relies on the number of clusters for $k$-integer weights. A second-pass algorithm is also provided to further optimize the core, leading to a reduced size proportional to $k$ for uniform weights. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness on real-world datasets. A companion paper explores an enhanced version with improved performance. Both versions have been made available online.

In large-scale grid worlds, efficient decision-making can be challenging, especially in scenarios with multiple agents and critical state transitions. To tackle this, the concept of superstates is used to aggregate adjacent states, reducing the search space while minimizing information loss. Previously, methods like MC search and value iteration were limited to small-scale applications due to their computationally intensive nature. We introduce a new approach, combining Monte Carlo estimation with linear quadratic regulation to optimize pursuit-evasion strategies in complex, high-dimensional grids. In doing so, we showcase superior performance compared to existing methods on sprawling grids alongside realistic, dynamically changing environments. Furthermore, our approach achieves remarkable results in scenarios featuring dynamic grid expansions and intricate state transitions, outperforming its predecessors and establishing a new standard for world understanding and action planning in pursuit-evasion scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate the capability to adapt quickly to unexpected changes, such as the sudden movement of an adversary or the appearance of a new evader. To investigate this concept, our research utilizes a Monte Carlo method to generate a range of rotational states within deformed halo nuclei by simulating the spin and orbital angular momentum of 1p-h pairing. Our findings indicate that the pairing interaction causes a rotation of the halo nucleus to assume a shape with an oval cross-section, oriented perpendicular to the direction of rotation. A central dense region with little change, surrounded by a more extensive and thinner deformation, characterizes the density distribution when compared to non-rotating halo nuclei. By utilizing this Monte Carlo method, we identify specific rotational states within these nuclei that exhibit halo characteristics. Recently, video super-resolution has seen significant advancements, but existing models often compromise quality for faster inference or vice versa. To address this limitation, we present BasicVSR++, a highly efficient and accurate video super-resolution model, which achieves a 2.79x speed-up while surpassing the PSNR performance of the original model by 0.13 dB. By refining the input frames and integrating temporal information, BasicVSR++ demonstrates a 0.16 dB gain in PSNR over the baseline model with only a 1.01x increase in computational complexity. Furthermore, our method achieves a notable 0.46 dB improvement in PSNR on the Real-World Super-Resolution Dataset, a commonly challenging benchmark. Implementing a self-guided spatial refinement module, BasicVSR++ successfully avoids introducing external items and achieves impressive results on the PIRM Real-World Super-Resolution Challenge, ranking second with a score of 0.407. Our code and model will be publicly available at https://github.com/zeangco/BasicVSR++.

When applying a single learned dynamics model across multiple reinforcement learning tasks, it may happen that the model is distorted by extraneous skills, leading to a decline in performance on the original task. To address this issue, we propose using multiple separate dynamics models for each task. However, selecting the best policy based on these models raises significant challenges. The problem becomes one of balancing exploration and identification of a suitable model, especially when the models vary greatly in quality. To tackle this, we suggest an algorithm that uses a distinct set of agents, each working with a different model, to achieve a balance of exploration and minimal regret. We also establish a theoretical bound for the total regret in the multi-task scenario. Additionally, our method achieves better results in practice, either by reducing the total regret or requiring a significantly smaller number of agents, especially in scenarios with significant variations in model performance. We provide experimental evidence to support our findings and demonstrate the comparative advantages of our approach over alternative methods. The code for our algorithm and accompanying experiments is available online.

This paper examines how the presence of compact boundaries affects the solution behavior of partial differential equations and differential systems on noncompact manifolds. By establishing an inequality related to the boundary distance, we obtain a global energy inequality for solutions to differential equations and differential systems. This enables us to apply standard parabolic regularization to approximate irregular solutions on the noncompact manifold. An alternative approach is to treat the compact boundary as part of a compact manifold that includes the boundary and the space outside of it, thereby applying standard elliptic boundary theory. Finally, we apply these methods to prove the existence of weak solutions to a specific partial differential equation. 

Keywords: Partial differential equations - Compact boundary - Noncompact manifold - Global energy inequality - Weak solution - Existence proof.

In 1936, Rosser enhanced Godel's first incompleteness theorem by demonstrating that in any formal system capable of basic arithmetic, there exists a statement  which can be formulated as both 'if F then not F' and 'either F or not F'. What is of considerable interest is that F can be structured to resemble a fundamental statement of the form 'x is an equation' within the formal system. Furthermore, a crucial aspect of Rosser's proof involves the utilization of a specific operator capable of intensifying the magnitude of F's satisfiability by no more than a finite amount. In this paper, a distinct, more general form of this operator is developed, and in doing so, the existing literature on first-order logic is being expanded to incorporate a broader range of operator structures. A key feature of this enhanced form involves the capability of intensifying the magnitude of F's satisfiability by an infinite degree, leading to the capacity to formulate statements of a more complex nature within the formal system. Consequently, this results in an instance where F's satisfiability cannot be equivalently captured by means of the original operator structure. In effect, this implies that the formal system itself is inherently incomplete, giving rise to a situation where it is possible to derive the intensification of a statement that is known to be unsatisfiable, thereby providing a new form of the first incompleteness theorem. In addition, this intensification operator also gives rise to a new type of paradoxical statement within the formal system, effectively serving as an alternative to Russell's paradoxical statement 'the set of all sets that do not contain themselves does contain itself'. Moreover, this intensification operator also gives rise to a new type of diagonalization operator, effectively serving as an alternative to Kleene's first completeness theorem for finite trees. Lastly, this intensification operator also gives rise to a new form of the second incompleteness theorem, effectively implying that if F can be formulated as 'either x is an equation or not' within the formal system, and F is known to be unsatisfiable, then this formal system will not derive a contradiction from intensifying F's satisfiability a finite amount. However, this result is no longer universally applicable when the intensification of F's satisfiability is allowed to be intensified an infinite amount. In this case, there exists a subclass of formal systems within which it is possible to derive a contradiction even when F is known to be unsatisfiable, giving rise to a new form of the second incompleteness theorem. In this work, we first provide an overview of Hadamard's three circles theorem for functions that are analytically continued within specific domains. Following that, we offer an investigation into the applicability of his method to functions that are monogenic in higher dimensions, aided by an assessment of the growth of such functions. Next, we establish the extension of Hadamard's three circles theorem to functions that are monogenic in higher dimensions by exploring its application to functions that are bounded and analytic within circular regions. Finally, we offer an evaluation of the relationship between the radius of the circle and the growth of functions that are monogenic in higher dimensions. Some specific cases, including functions that are harmonic in higher dimensions, are also considered. In those cases, we establish sharper estimates. In the case of functions that are harmonic in three-dimensional space, such estimates were previously obtained by Schoen and Souplet in their work from 2011. In the case of functions that are harmonic in four-dimensional space, such estimates were previously obtained by the author in his work from 2019. In the case of functions that are harmonic in five-dimensional space, such estimates are presented here for the first time. Some open questions are also proposed within this work. This research is an extension of my Ph.D. thesis, which was completed at Aalto University under the supervision of Rainer Kähler in 2020. Those estimates were previously obtained by Henrik Shahmadi in his work from 2019, but only under the additional assumption that the functions in question have a specific bound on their rotation. It's also interesting to note that our model can still produce accurate results even with no labels during training, leveraging the capabilities of self-supervised image understanding. By leveraging an alternative distance metric with a regularization, we successfully trained this GAN to produce accurate and varied posterior estimates, effectively augmenting and completing sparse data sets, ultimately leading to realistic reconstructed images.
