As terahertz frequencies become more accessible, wireless links are beginning to take advantage of this technology to create high-rate data transmission paths. One issue with implementing terahertz links is their limited range, which means they often require multiple hops to travel significant distances. While implementing beam training across each hop could mitigate performance degradation, it would significantly increase training time. Instead, we propose dynamic beam training for multi-hop terahertz links, which allows for optimized training across each hop. Through simulation, we show our approach not only rivals traditional beam training methods in performance but also reduces training time by as much as 75%. Additionally, we've established theoretical limits for our proposed method and found it could increase link efficiency by up to 3.5 dB. We also evaluated our solution under real-world scenarios and found it could improve performance by as much as 25%. Further, we've established that the worst-case performance with our method is no worse than -0.8 dB compared to ideal performance. Finally, we've determined that our method can handle up to four hops without significant performance degradation. However, very large networks may require different optimization strategies. Through our proposals and findings, we aim to lay the groundwork for efficient multi-hop terahertz links, and we're providing our code for further research and development. Advances in wireless communication are often driven by the development of new technologies, and we believe our work can accelerate the adoption of terahertz frequencies in wireless systems. While our research focuses on multi-hop terahertz links, our methods can be applied to other bandwidth-hopping systems, and we're eager to explore more applications in the future. As a result of this work, we've developed novel algorithms for efficient beam training, and we're open to collaboration with researchers and industry professionals to bring these solutions to market. Ultimately, our goal is to serve as a starting point for further research and to play a key role in the widespread adoption of terahertz frequencies. To this end, we're providing our code on an open-source basis, along with detailed simulations and real-world implementations, along with relevant theoretical bounds, through an interactive Jupyter notebook that can be accessed via an accompanying paper. We've observed radio signal interference around a specific point in the sky,
specifically around the location of the binary pulsar PSR B1133+16.  By analyzing
data from three different radio telescopes, we've identified multiple radio
sources, identified as scattering screens, at specific distances from Earth.
Combining these results with the pulsar's exact location, we've calculated the
coordinates of the scattering screens in the sky.  Interestingly, one of the
screens lies almost exactly 180 degrees opposite the pulsar.  We believe this
may indicate that this screen could be part of a large structure extending
between the Earth and the pulsar, possibly related to a wall or a filament.
Further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis and to learn more about
this possible connection.  We also found that one of the screens has a higher
than expected density, which could indicate that this screen may be made up
of smaller clusters.  Finally, we were able to use the movement of the screens
against the background of quasars to estimate their distance from Earth,
concluding that they are located far beyond the Galactic Center.  This finding
has significant implications for the study of scattering screens and may lead to
a reevaluation of current understanding of this phenomenon.  Our observations
also vary the screens' density with their distance from Earth, which may indicate
that density decreases with distance.  This discovery could be key to
developing a statistical model of scattering screens.  We've found that using
multi-frequency observations can help distinguish genuine scattering interference
from other sources of radio noise, which could be beneficial for future pulsar
research.  Finally, we've established a statistical basis for identifying
scattering screens, which can be used to confirm the validity of our findings
and to test our hypotheses in future analyses.  This study is based on data
collected from the Parkes Radio Telescope in Australia and the Arecibo
Observatory in Puerto Rico, with additional support from the Green Bank
Telescope in West Virginia.  This research was funded by the National
Science Foundation and the National Research Council.  It is also part of a
larger project led by Professor Thomas Landecker, who pioneered the use of
wide-field radio observations and developed the technique used in this study.  
This research is significant because it represents a major breakthrough in the
use of scattering screens analysis and could be a crucial step towards a new
statistical model of this phenomenon.

Inspired by the human brain's organization, cascaded neural networks have gained popularity due to their effectiveness in complex tasks like speech and audio processing. Despite their success, implementing a neural network that can reliably generate entire seconds of coherent speech remains a challenge. This is because standard approaches typically fail to capture the quasi-periodic nature of speech, which is characterized by recurring patterns in time. To address this limitation, we propose a novel cascaded network architecture called the Temporal Cascade Recurrent Neural Network, which divides speech production into multiple overlapping segments, each modeled by a separate recurrent module. Connectors between these modules allow for the exchange of relevant contextual information, which can be spread over time. Through a process of contextual delay, the network is able to share features across different time segments, thus capturing the recurring patterns in speech. Our experiments show that this design achieves a significant improvement in performance, with a lower average frequency spectrum and a more natural speech rhythm, which is further verified by subjective listener tests. The proposed network's ability to model long-term temporal dependencies in speech is demonstrated through a series of evaluations, including comparisons with existing cascaded network architectures. Annotating large sets of textual data requires significant time and resources, 
making it crucial to develop effective technologies to streamline and enhance 
annotator efficiency. By providing context and relevant information from the 
text, we can simplify the annotation process by allowing annotators to focus 
on specific aspects within a larger document section. In this paper, we present 
a method for linking local annotations to surrounding context based on multiple 
factor combinations, and demonstrate its application to medical note annotation. 
Our approach incorporates two key components: (1) a neural network that pinpoints 
relevant context sections, and (2) a design for flexible context selection that 
can be applied across multiple domains. By evaluating our technique on real-world 
medical data, we were able to show that annotated objects can be accurately 
identified in surrounding text sections (F1 score: 0.76), and that the design 
can be applied across different datasets (F1 score: 0.83). Furthermore, we 
observed a significant reduction (x5) in annotation time when providing context. 
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing annotator 
efficiency and precision when working with large textual documents. In addition, 
we have introduced a publicly accessible dataset (PadChall-EMNRP) that includes 
annotated data linked to surrounding context, along with design prototypes, 
and have made the code and data available at this link https://github.com/flatmap-io/Context-Selection-EMNRP-Challenge.

We take topological Hochschild homology through the lens of its connection to the $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring perspective, examining how it interacts with bicategorical'shadows' that arise from the composition of monoidal functors between $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring spectra. By exploring this relationship, we establish links between topological Hochschild homology, its derived forms, and the Picard bicategory of topological $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring spectra, incorporating their relationships with bicategorical'shadows'. These links become particularly accessible via the topological Kahn-Remillard suspension theorem. Building on this foundation, we can then define and study variants of topological Hochschild homology within the context of bicategorical'shadows'. Finally, we can then establish connections with board games, obtaining computations for various shadows of topological Hochschild homology through their connections to the functors HH_*(-) and THH_*(−,−). 

This research is presented in three parts. In Part I, we review key concepts, including topological Hochschild homology, the Picard bicategory of topological $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring spectra, and the Kahn-Remillard suspension theorem. In Part II, we explore shadow functors, discussing both functors that produce shadows and those that extend shadow functors to functors between $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring spectra. In Part III, we study board games that correspond to shadow functors, computing various shadows of topological Hochschild homology through these games.

We introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), a comprehensive sound source localization benchmark consisting of 15,000 realistic source images and accompanying audio data, crafted by dynamically altering source positions around a still object in a controlled environment. Based on enhanced versions of the Fisher discriminant and iterative closest point algorithms, we developed a method to accurately predict source locations from visual and auditory data combined. Our approach, the VGG-Sound Source network, leverages advanced image processing features, incorporates auditory data using self-supervised learning, and is trained in a efficient manner with minimal adjustments. Compared to existing sound source localization datasets, VGG-SS features diverse and naturally occurring source types, objects, and backgrounds. Notably, our method achieves remarkable performance on this dataset, surpassing previous standards with high accuracy levels. Additionally, cross-dataset testing reveals our approach's robustness and ability to adapt to new sources and objects with relative ease. Recently, hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (HGCNs) have gained popularity due to their ability to represent multi-dimensional relationships between nodes. However, these methods are limited by their requirement for a fixed-dimensional space and a predetermined angle. This research develops the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), an innovative framework that enables nodes to have variable feature dimensions and learns the graph structure naturally. By incorporating a parameter learning approach, LGCN significantly enhances the accuracy of both node classification and link prediction tasks compared to existing HGCNs. Moreover, LGCN introduces a new method for enhancing the expressiveness of its representations, allowing it to capture rich contextual information. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of LGCN over multiple baseline methods. Additionally, a comparison between different parameter learning strategies is conducted to explore the benefits of variable feature dimensions in graph neural networks. We propose a concept for a hybrid optomechanical system that incorporates both photon-phonon and electron-spin interactions to create a combined optoelectromechanical system. This system allows for the visualization of single-electron tunneling spatial symmetry, and through proper design, can produce a tunneling spatial symmetry effect even in the absence of tunneling. A theoretical model is developed to describe the behavior of this system, and we demonstrate experimentally using scanning tunneling microscopy on a Pt/Si(111) surface. The results show that tunneling electron spatial symmetry can be modulated optically, and this effect could be useful for controlling single-electron tunneling via optical means. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this system enables direct optical modulation of a mechanical resonance frequency in a Pt/Si mechanical system. Additionally, we show that this system allows for the creation of spatially-symmetric mechanical modes in a Si mechanical system, and we visualize the single-electron tunneling spatial symmetry effect in this system. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this technology in quantum manipulation and measurement.

We explore an extension of $u$-calculus, dubbed $\mu$-calculus with atoms, which incorporates both program counter and atom parameters within its recursive formulas. In this study, we examine the individual components of this expression, first treating the program counter in isolation from atoms, then considering their collective interplay. When the program counter is isolated, we find that the resulting system possesses an infinite number of satisfiable instances despite being decidable. In contrast, the presence of both program counter and atoms renders the system undecidable, outperforming the expressive capacity of $u$-calculus while matching that of $\mu$-calculus. However, when atoms are allowed to influence one another, we demonstrate a finite, yet complex, satisfiable instance. Additionally, we develop decision procedures for both decidable fragments and showcase the theoretical relationships between these systems via bisimulation connections. These developments provide novel insights into the complex dynamics underlying $\mu$-calculus with atoms. As a result, this language offers a more versatile framework for modeling a broader spectrum of properties in directed graphs. We examine the generalized Tsallis distribution across multiple domains, including physics, economics, and biology. By drawing on examples such as econophysics, where Tsallis statistics may aid our comprehension of financial market behavior and instability, and biology, where Tsallis distribution is utilized to analyze and propose models for describing non-linear dynamics in gene expression, we illustrate its applicability and utility. Furthermore, we explore social systems that follow the Tsallis distribution, for which we propose a simple decision-making model that incorporates memory and bias. The resulting equations can be transformed into a fractional Brownian motion, providing insight into the path to power law behavior and the potential for comparing social dynamics with natural processes that follow similar patterns. Additionally, we discuss how Tsallis statistics can be utilized in the analysis of complex networks, offering a broader perspective on the use of this distribution in understanding systems composed of interacting elements in both social and biological contexts. Lastly, we emphasize the importance of considering memory effects when interpreting data fitted with the Tsallis distribution, given that many natural processes exhibit a high level of persistence that can be mistaken for long-tailed behavior. In the realm of social dynamics, we suggest that our model can serve as a starting point for further study, particularly in addressing how memory and bias contribute to the emergence of power law behavior in a broader range of applications. In so doing, we provide a theoretical foundation for using the Tsallis distribution in the analysis of complex systems, which in turn is rooted in a broader set of principles that govern self-organized systems in both social and physical contexts. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for applying this framework across a range of systems, including financial networks, life sciences, and planetary science. In doing, we set the stage for a multidisciplinary exploration of power law behavior, which holds significant implications for our comprehension of processes that exhibit long-term persistence and extreme event occurrence. In this study, we offer an initial foray into this research direction, which we believe positions itself at the nexus of multiple-domain research, all of which revolves around the central question of when social systems follow the Tsallis distribution and what this entails for our understanding of complex behavior in this domain. In so doing, we aim to spark a broader discussion among researchers from multiple domains, which in turn can contribute to the development of a more unified theoretical framework for exploring power law behavior in complex systems. Recently, Cai and Zhang proved that approximating a certain class of double covers of signed graphs involves a NP-hard combinatorial problem. Building on this finding, we examine parametrized approximation algorithms for another class of double covers known as extended double covers of signed graphs. Specifically, we show that even finding a 2/3 approximation requires at least O(n^2) time on a Turing machine limited to n^2 bits. Since planar-completeness can occur in a more complex setting, we cannot rule out the possibility that approximating extended double covers of signed graphs is complete in a class of problems that can be solved in a limited number of steps for graphs on a flat surface. However, we do demonstrate that approximating extended double covers of signed graphs is manageable when the input graph has a limited number of vertices. Furthermore, we can determine an exact solution in a reasonable time frame for a specific case where the target value is known. This case involves finding extended double covers of signed graphs that can be colored using a specific number of colors. Hybrid quantum dynamics is categorized into four types: Hamiltonian, thermo-hybrid, quantum hydrodynamics, and quantum thermo-hydrodynamics. We have established a broad equilibrium theory for quantum systems, covering all these dynamics. Specifically, we have defined and characerized quantum hydrodynamics and thermo-hydrodynamics equilibrium conditions. These conditions can be understood as dynamical mean field theories for the relevant hybrid dynamics. We have also developed a robust numerical algorithm for calculating quantum hydrodynamics and thermo-hydrodynamics quantities. Our study provides a framework for studying quantum complex systems, and offers a bridge between thermodynamic and dynamical approaches. Moreover, it enables the investigation of quantum systems under influence from external time-dependent drives. We have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach with an example involving a simple model with a coherent drive. Our results show that quantum hydrodynamics and thermo-hydrodynamics can accurately capture nonequilibrium phenomena even in situations where the system's behavior is critically linked to the phase of the drive. This is achievable without resolving the dynamic mean field theory in the time-domain. Instead, we have applied a Wigner transform approach that directly utilizes the Hamiltonian and relates the equilibrium correlations to currents that develop over half-cycles of the drive. This approach provides valuable physical insights into quantum hydrodynamics and thermo-hydrodynamics and may be expanded to include additional degrees of freedom. Moreover, it paves the way for further generalizations, such as incorporating fluctuations that are now being researched. Our study is also expected to lay the groundwork for improving dynamical mean field theories by taking into consideration the connections between different spectral weights that emerge when studying quantum systems under the influence of time-dependent drives. Ultimately, this is expected to lead to more accurate descriptions of the spectra of quantum systems that exhibit robust spectral weight at the Fermi level, such as cuprates which have non-trivial Fermi surfaces. These systems display distinct spectral features, including sharp coherent peaks, tunelling, and charge transfer edges, as well as broad coherence gaps, and have complex spectral landscapes that are difficult to model using traditional dynamical mean field theory methods alone. We invite readers to step into the fascinating realm of negative temperatures where their basic understanding can be put to the test. To facilitate comprehension, we introduce a simple two-level system representation, equivalent to a spin-1/2 particle, and illustrate key concepts including thermal equilibrium, cooling mechanisms, and the preparation of negative temperatures. We then apply this foundation to explore in-depth the behavior of systems consisting of interacting two-level units, focusing particularly on Swanson's system of negatively tempered bosons and the phenomenon of negative temperature cat state creation. A two-level system analogy is also used to analyze counter-flow between two boson samples at different temperatures. A theoretical model involving dipoles interacting with a common optical wave is presented to describe these phenomena. We also discuss experimental demonstration of these complex temperature phenomena. Finally, we discuss open system dynamics and propose a negative temperature multi-meson system as an suitable target for generalizing counter-flow theory.

Let $A$ be a nonempty finite subset of integers, and $k$ any integer. The restricted sumset of $A$ is defined as $\sigma_k(A) = \{a_1 + \cdots + a_n \mid a_i \in A, n \in \mathbb{N}, n \equiv k \pmod{2}\}$. Recently, a significant advancement was made in understanding the size of restricted sumsets in relation to additive combinatorial techniques. Building upon earlier work of Smith and Shakan, we demonstrate that for any nonempty finite subset of integers $A$, the cardinality of its restricted sumset $\sigma_k(A)$ exceeds $|A|^2$ except in instances where $A$ features a particular structural pattern centered around an integer $m$ with a multiplicity of $1$, in which case $\sigma_k(A)$ may be smaller than $|A|^2$ only when $k$ is equivalent to $0$ modulo the greatest common divisor of the coefficients defining the structure of the set and is no larger than the number of coefficients expressing the distinct elements of $A$ summed to $m$. Moreover, the applicability of this result to $k$ equivalence classes is also established. Ultimately, this advancement paves the way for further exploration into the dynamics of growth in restricted sumsets. In addition, new instances of sets with small sumsets are identified, and in particular, a larger class of minimal large sumsets within the context of abelian groups. These findings introduce new concepts and edifices of near-minimal large sumsets, thereby expanding the realm of this significant area of research. The traditional T-H method has several limitations when dealing with high-frequency problems, primarily stemming from its narrow frequency band and the requirement for a minimum six points per wavelength. A new, enhanced formulation of the T-H surface formulation addresses these constraints by transforming the problem into a system of linear equations. This approach, which leverages the local behavior of polynomials, enables the use of smaller sample sizes, thereby improving computational efficiency. A new formulation of the T-H method specifically for acoustic scattering problems has been developed, which eliminates the need for discrete elements and significantly simplifies the simulation process. This method has been demonstrated through numerical examples, including a comprehensive investigation of acoustic scattering from an array of perfectly conducting cylinders under plane wave excitation. The results obtained from the new formulation are compared to those of the traditional NNI method and validated through direct numerical simulations. A discussion on the applicability and scalability of the proposed method to larger-scale simulations is also presented. A Fortran-based code incorporating an adaptive quadrule method for integrating the far-field patterns has been developed and shown to be both accurate and efficient. Ultimately, this novel approach provides a robust framework for simulating acoustic scattering phenomena. The source code accompanying this paper is available online. These measurements were compared with that of water content in Antarctic finds of the same stone type, showing a significantly higher water content in the Antarctic finds than in the recent fallen specimens, with a significant disparity of nearly two times the value measured in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk. Water content in Tagish Lake exhibited a water content of 0.52±0.09 wt.%, whereas in the Antarctic finds it was 0.85±0.09, 0.82±0.09, 0.78±0.09, 1.45±0.09, 1.26±0.09 and 0.75±0.09 wt.%. It is worth noting that the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, fallen in 2018 and 2013 respectively, exceeded the average Earth crust water content, transforming them into Earth's water richest fallen objects. Building from the fundamental principles of integrable physics, we create a comprehensive framework for studying XXZ chains with higher spins and multiple sites. Our framework, which includes scalar products, form factors and correlation functions for generic values of spin and site, is systematically established through cumulative developments. Notably, our work first obtains generic scalar products for the spin-1/2 XXZ chain, extends existing forms factor findings to all on-site spins and subsequently derives correlation functions via a cumulant expansion. Secondly, inspired by existing spin-1/2 chain results, our work directly obtains generic form factors for the spin-1 XXZ chain by integrating the conformal field theory approach and anti-automorphism property of the Hamiltonian. Finally, our study expands correlation functions beyond cumulant approximation. Both the spin-1/2 and spin-1 cases allow us to analyze chain properties, validate lattice versions of field theory predictions and reveal unexpected behaviors. Lastly, our framework paves the way for similar investigations in higher-spin spin chains with impurities or interacting domains. Several important results have emerged from applying our framework, including a precise expression for the scalar product of two spin states in the spin-1/2 XXZ chain, detailed structure factors for the spin-1 XXZ chain and novel correlation functions for both chains. These discoveries significantly enhance our understanding of these models and may also provide relevant insights into the physics of similar systems. Notably, several key results have already been verified through direct numerical calculations in spin chain contexts. Furthermore, our framework has implications for developing a more comprehensive theory of integrable systems and their applications. Several research paths are identified for further exploration, such as extending the framework to higher-spin chains with impurities or interacting domains, creating a more general cumulant expansion applicable to multiple spins and developing a cumulative approach to form factor calculations. Ultimately, this study positions itself at the forefront of a new wave of research aimed at thoroughly analyzing the properties of integrable higher-spin XXZ chains through a unified framework, giving due credit to previous related works. Our proposed framework, Efficient Zero-Source Speech Translation, introduces a new paradigm for speech translation that eliminates the need for source speech and reduces the necessary data to less than 32 sentences. This model leverages pre-trained components and mutates the encoder and decoder to adapt to new languages and sources. By introducing a new multi-source encoder and a language adapter for the decoder, our framework achieves significant gains in speech translation accuracy in few-shot settings. The proposed teacher-student learning technique and mutual learning approach further enhance performance. Our results show substantial improvements in speech translation accuracy in few-shot settings, with models reaching 19.3 BLEU scores in the CoSum dataset and 22.8 in the CTS dataset, an improvement of 4.4 and 11.2 BLEU points respectively. The code and data will be made available to the public.

We introduce Generalized Spherical Multipoles (GSMs), a flexible generalization of conventional multipoles that can be any order and either whole-number-ordered or complex. Our analysis shows that such multipoles effectively capture electromagnetic scattering, even in a random environment, outperforming all other methods. Our method involves correlating the multipoles with electromagnetic fields at different points, which we demonstrate can be done locally using far-field properties. Our findings also reveal that the multipoles' time-average energy growth follows a simple pattern, powered by the square of their wavenumber. Moreover, we find that the multipoles' time-average energy can be used to measure their dimensionless volume. Our method's versatility allows it to apply to any system with non-zero dimensionless volume, regardless of its symmetry. Finally, we apply our method to study the scattering of light from dielectric particles and ensembles of particles, which we believe will contribute to a better understanding of scattering problems. Our method provides a universal way to describe electromagnetic scattering from any system with non-zero dimensionless volume, and we hope it to be a valuable tool for tackling complex radiation problems. Additionally, we identify potential applications for this approach, including the improvement of superdirectivity techniques.

A recent discovery established a link between Schur elements and shifted Schur polynomials under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. Building upon this finding, we demonstrate that this correspondence holds true for a broader range of functions categorized by the Schur process. Furthermore, we incorporate the dual perspective to demonstrate the extended interconnection is compatible with the eigenvalue distributions of random Hermitian matrices in various symplectic and orthogonal ensemble categories. This matrix theory framework is further demonstrated to be analogous to the Schur process, thereby solidifying the extension of the initial observation made under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. Our discovery is supported by both analytical and numerical evidence. We also present the theoretical basis for our extended harmonic sum representation of the shifted Schur process. Additionally, we showcase the applicability of this representation to derive moment inequalities, which can be further utilized to derive a broader range of distributional results for the Schur process and its shifted counterpart. Our method is particularly adaptable to capturing the interconnections seen within the Harish-Chandra isomorphism setting. We also explore connections between the Schur process and various Hermitian matrix models by obtaining an explicit expression for scalar field correlations in an orthogonal ensemble with a symplectic ensemble's eigenvalue distributions, thereby establishing a bridge between these two branches of random matrix theory. This achievement is also visible within the Harish-Chandra isomorphism framework. Our study is further accompanied by a comprehensive set of results that can be utilized to derive the limiting behavior of various distribution-related parameters in both the Schur process and its shifted counterpart, as well as in corresponding models of random Hermitian matrices. Some of these results can be utilized to derive moment inequalities, which can be applied to derive distributional results in a broader range of settings. Adding a minimal dark sector to a seesaw model breaks the four-dimensional bulk modulus symmetry, potentially making the vacuum unstable. However, if we limit the dark sector to have the same parity as the bulk, the stability of the vacuum is preserved. This approach also eliminates the problem of dark energy in the model. Utilizing an entropic component with a dark fluid parity constraint, we find that the temperature of the universe remains very close to the desired value, around 3.36 K. Furthermore, the model predicts a specific scale for the first inflationary transition, around 1.8 times the present-day cosmological scale, which is in line with the predictions of multiverse scenarios. The model's first inflationary transition has a distinctive signature in the form of gravitational waves with a nearly flat amplitude in the range of 10^(-7) to 10^(-5). The model also forecasts the occurrence of gravitational waves with a nearly circular polarization in the range of 10^(-7) to 10^(-5). The model's predictions for the spectrum of primordial perturbations are within the allowed ranges of the Planck and other experiments' findings. The model forecasts the occurrence of multiparticle decays in the first inflationary transition, which could result in the production of light sterile neutrinos and Kosinsky axions. The model also forecasts the occurrence of gravitational waves with a specific frequency and amplitude in the range of 10^(-5). The model predicts that the next inflationary transition will have a significant impact on the universe, including the creation of new dimensions, the production of dark matter and dark energy, and a significant change in the universe's overall energy density. The model forecasts that this transition will occur within the next 10^10 to 10^11 years. The model also forecasts that this transition will be accompanied by a significant increase in the universe's temperature, potentially causing the universe to enter a phase of rapid expansion similar to inflation. The model's predictions for the occurrence of gravitational waves, multiparticle decays, light sterile neutrinos, Kosinsky axions, and a rapid increase in temperature provide testable hypotheses that can be verified or discounted through the study of gravitational waves and the distribution of matter and energy in the universe. We calculate the spin-orbit coupling strength in transition metal oxides using a effective model, considering the interactions of d-orbitals with s and p-electrons from neighboring atoms, as well as the crystal field splitting within the d-shell. Our expression for SOC is a sum of two parts: one arising from d-electron interaction with neighboring s and p-electrons through the exchange potential, and the other due to the difference in one-electron energies within the d-shell. These two contributions correlate with the Hartree energy and the effective charge of d-electrons, respectively. Our results apply to 3d, 4d, and 5d materials, and we examine the variability of SOC in these classes of materials. We find that SOC in 3d-series materials can be understood by the small effective mass of d-electrons, whereas in 4d and 5d materials, it's influenced by the mixing of d-orbitals with neighboring s and p-orbitals that widen the d-band and boost d-soc. Finally, we distinguish between intrinsically isolated and weakly coupled materials, and propose that SOC might be an important factor in superconductivity among the latter group. Our study is concluded with an examination of s-wave and d-wave superconductivity within the BCS framework, and our results are applicable to a range of materials including cuprates and pnictides. Ultimately, we contend that SOC is a crucial component that should be incorporated into the phase diagram of these materials. Our research is further expanded to consider other materials with exceptional SOC strength, such as WTe$_2$, and is supplemented by a discussion on the relevance of SOC to these materials' electrical conductivity. Ultimately, we propose that our SOC model may be adapted to study topological insulators and semimetals, such as WTe$_2$, by integrating it with the Dirac/Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our study is finally extended to the quantum regime, and we demonstrate that SOC may be understood through the topological quantum chemistry campaign by summing the weights of orbital waves at high energy. This topological understanding of SOC is applicable across all three series of transition metal oxides, and we contend that it may be employed to study other materials with exceptional SOC strength. We derive a relationship between the relative $I$-functions of toric complete intersections with smooth divisors, expressing one in terms of the others. This relationship is expressed through a determinant formula involving the relative $I$-functions and the weights of the projective embedding. Furthermore, we establish an alternative formula for the relative $I$-functions through a Laplace transform of the classical $I$-functions, and demonstrate its connection to the hypergeometric functions defined over the orthogonality lattices of the integers. We also examine the compatibility of the relative $I$-functions under the change of variables, and present examples to illustrate these concepts. Finally, we propose that the relative $I$-functions are allied with multiple zeta values, and discuss potential directions for further study. This research is motivated by the goals of clarifying the properties of the relative $I$-functions, and exploring their connection to values of multiple zeta values. It is with great sadness that we acknowledge the guidance and contributions of Hiroshi Sunouchi to these results, as he has passed away during the course of this research.

Deep generative models like GANs and VAEs have significantly advanced image creation and the development of novel tools for manipulating digital data. Crucially, these applications lie at the intersection of computer vision and medical imaging. For example, hospitals could utilize a model that predicts patient outcomes by analyzing images, leveraging the embedded representation for improved risk assessment. However, most existing models fail to achieve accurate predictions and retain the underlying context. In this research, we introduce Area-Code Network (ACN), a generative adversarial model that produces detailed medical images with a focused representation. This representation can be easily modified to produce similar images, thereby enabling reliable outcome prediction. By incorporating an auxiliary encoder that identifies the underlying context and contributes to the representation, we ve achieved a notable increase in both image quality and classification accuracy. Our results demonstrate significant advancements in both areas when using the commonly employed evaluation metrics. Most importantly, our method achieves superior outcome prediction performance when using real outcome data, outperforming alternative approaches by a substantial margin. To facilitate reproducibility and progress in the field, we've made our code and datasets available publicly. Our work presents a novel concept of context representation in medical imaging and sets the stage for the exploration of context modification. This could enable innovative applications such as planning surgical interventions and tailoring treatment options based on patient-specific conditions. Advanced data visualization is crucial in exploring and navigating complex, high-dimensional data. Many powerful tools for dimension reduction, such as t-SNE and UMAP, have gained widespread acceptance, but often their outcomes are difficult to interpret for non-experts. To address this limitation, we've developed ViDaExpert, an interactive web application that enables users to easily visualize and analyze multiple-dimensional data plots generated by popular reduction techniques. ViDaExpert can be utilized in conjunction with popular programming languages like R and Python, and is particularly designed to complement popular visualization tools like ggplot2 and Matplotlib. By integrating a variety of features that enhance visualization and exploration, including clickable dimensions, color coding, zooming, and region highlighting, ViDaExpert significantly enhances the understanding and analysis of high-dimensional data. Additionally, it facilitates the comparison of different reduction approaches and data preprocessing techniques. Given its interactive and user-friendly interface, ViDaExpert is an invaluable resource for data analysts, researchers, and scientists to present their findings more effectively to audiences who may not be familiar with high-dimensional data visualization. ViDaExpert is now available as a user-friendly web application, along with a comprehensive API, at this link: https://vidaexpert.tluminski.com/. Its source code is openly accessible on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/tluminski/ViDaExpert. ViDaExpert has unique capabilities that set it apart from other web-based visualizers, including customized interaction tools and multi-dimensional exploration features, as demonstrated in our application note. This research focuses on developing a high-order two-dimensional monomial approximation using Lagrange polynomials and a set of reference points. The new approach can be an alternative to using tensor product bases with high degrees or a Lagrange basis with a large number of points. By constructing this approximation, we can still ensure that it satisfies the given boundary conditions. We have investigated two scenarios for selecting the set of monomials: one with a minimum number of terms that can capture a given function within a specific error margin, and another with a set of terms that allows for a precise approximation. We used a variety of test functions to analyze how the size of the mesh element, the type of polynomial used, and the specific function being approximated impact the accuracy of this new approach. Additionally, we have compared our results to those obtained from a similar study, one that used a different method to construct these approximations. Our findings demonstrate that this new method can produce highly accurate approximations, often with a much smaller number of terms. We have also found that when a fine mesh is used, the optimal approximation often yields a very low error, typically on the order of $10^{-12}$ when using double precision. However, this does not guarantee stability for all cases, and we have encountered situations where the optimal approximation resulted in a significantly higher error, sometimes even exceeding the initial estimate by several orders of magnitude. To better understand these unstable instances, we have conducted additional analyses, including exploring connections between the eigenvalues of the approximation matrix and the condition number of the Jacobian matrix that maps the monomial mesh to the original mesh. Our research has also confirmed that the new method can be an effective tool for approximating functions that satisfy non-homogeneous boundary conditions, even those with sharp corners. We have validated this by comparing our results to both a high-order finite element method and a Lagrange polynomial approach with a larger number of points. Lastly, we have applied this new approach to two different inverse problems: an inverse boundary value problem and an optimal control problem. Our results demonstrate that this method can produce accurate approximations of the state and control variables, even in situations where the input data is limited. Nonetheless, we have also observed instances where this approach can become stuck in local minima, and we have considered several alternative strategies to mitigate this issue. Finally, we have recognized that this new approach has the potential to be efficient for solving large-scale problems, but we have not yet explored its fully parallelized potential.
